set_title: CLAT PG Practice Set 03 (Committees and Commissions, Linked Amendments and Judgments; Trap-Annotated)

pattern.ordering: Each passage runs committee/commission -> law or amendment -> judgments, across the whole CLAT PG syllabus
pattern.note: Practice set, not a mock; original passages and questions (none taken from Mock 01-06, Practice Set 01 or 02). The official paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes; this set is longer for extra practice.

subjects_covered: Constitutional Law (Constituent Assembly and Constitutional Review)
Constitutional Law and Family Law (Uniform Civil Code)
Medical Law, Torts and Constitutional Law
instructions: Each question has four options and exactly one correct answer.
Correct answer carries 1 mark; each wrong answer carries -0.25.

Passages are original summaries for practice, current to mid-November 2026. Verify pending or evolving matters (e.g. the Election Commissioners Appointment Act challenge, the IBC Amendment Bill 2025, the All India Judges Association practice rule, the labour code rules, BNS s.152 challenge) against current official sources.
Every explanation includes why the other options fail, the CLAT trap, and any language trick.

passages.title: Law Commission Reports on Death Penalty, Hate Speech and Sedition
passages.passage: The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory advisory body whose reports are persuasive and do not bind Parliament or the courts. In its 262nd Report (2015), it recommended abolition of the death penalty for all offences other than those related to terrorism, in particular waging war against the State. In its 267th Report (2017) on hate speech, it proposed two new provisions in the Penal Code, sections 153C and 505A, to punish incitement to discrimination and the causing of fear or alarm. In its 279th Report (2023) on sedition, it recommended that section 124A be retained with procedural safeguards, including a preliminary inquiry by a police officer of at least the rank of Inspector before an FIR is registered. The courts had by then spoken on all three subjects. In Bachan Singh (1980), a Constitution Bench by a 4:1 majority upheld the death penalty but confined it to the rarest of rare cases, requiring special reasons under section 354(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code and a balance of aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Machhi Singh (1983) later classified the categories of such cases. In Shatrughan Chauhan (2014), the Court held that inordinate and unexplained delay in deciding a mercy petition, which the President or the Governor decides under Articles 72 and 161, is a ground for commuting a death sentence under Article 21. In Manoj v State of Madhya Pradesh (2022), the Court stressed the duty to collect mitigation material before sentence. In Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan (2014), the Court declined to legislate on hate speech and asked the Law Commission to examine the matter. In Kedar Nath Singh (1962), section 124A was upheld only so far as it punishes incitement to violence or a tendency to public disorder; in S.G. Vombatkere (2022), the Court kept the section in abeyance, stayed pending proceedings and restrained fresh FIRs. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 has since replaced section 124A with section 152; challenges to that section may be pending (verify current status).

questions.question: On the passage, the recommendation of the 262nd Report on the death penalty

options.A: does not bind Parliament or the courts, because a Law Commission report is only persuasive
options.B: lapses automatically if Parliament does not act on it within two sessions after its submission to the Government
options.C: binds Parliament once the report is laid before it, since the Commission is a body constituted under the Constitution
options.D: binds sentencing courts, because Bachan Singh required them to follow the Commission's views on capital punishment

questions.explanation: The passage says the Commission is non-statutory and its reports are persuasive, so Parliament remains free to retain capital punishment for any offence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B gives the Commission a constitutional status and binding force that it lacks. Option C invents a link between Bachan Singh and the Commission. Option D invents a lapse rule.
questions.clat_trap: Law Commission reports are often mistaken for law because the topic is a hot issue. The test is the status of a recommendation, not its popularity.
questions.language_trick: 'persuasive' is the key word; binding and lapsing are the distractors.

questions.question: A death-row convict's mercy petition has remained undecided for years without explanation. On the passage, his best ground is that

options.A: the death sentence can now be executed only after the Law Commission records a fresh recommendation on the case
options.B: the delay makes the conviction itself void, because the trial court loses jurisdiction over a sentence not executed in time
options.C: the Governor alone may now decide the petition, since the President's power under Article 72 lapses with delay
options.D: inordinate and unexplained delay in deciding it can justify commutation of the death sentence into a lesser one under Article 21

questions.explanation: Shatrughan Chauhan treats unexplained delay as a ground for commutation under Article 21. It does not void the conviction or shift the power.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attacks the conviction, whereas the delay affects only the sentence. Option B invents a lapse of the President's power. Option C wrongly gives the Commission a role in individual cases.
questions.clat_trap: The mercy power under Articles 72 and 161 is mentioned, which tempts a student to shift power between authorities.
questions.language_trick: 'sentence' vs 'conviction': delay touches only the former.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The sections 153C and 505A proposed in the 267th Report are law in force against hate speech. Reason (R): In Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan, the Supreme Court asked the Law Commission to examine hate speech instead of legislating itself.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The 267th Report only proposed the provisions, so A is false. R is true, as the Court declined to legislate and asked the Law Commission to examine the matter.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A treats a proposal as an enactment. R is a correct statement that sounds like the explanation for A, but it explains the Court's restraint, not any law in force.
questions.clat_trap: Students read R as the cause of A because both concern hate speech and the Commission.
questions.language_trick: 'proposed' in the passage vs 'law in force' in A.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes Kedar Nath Singh (1962) from S.G. Vombatkere (2022)?

options.A: Kedar Nath upheld section 124A on a narrow reading, while Vombatkere merely suspended its operation without striking it down
options.B: Both decisions upheld the section, but they differed on whether an FIR may be registered on the basis of a preliminary inquiry by police
options.C: Kedar Nath kept the section in abeyance pending a larger Bench, while Vombatkere read it down to incitement to violence and public disorder
options.D: Kedar Nath struck down section 124A as unconstitutional, while Vombatkere revived it with the safeguard of an inquiry by an Inspector-rank officer

questions.explanation: Kedar Nath confined the section to incitement to violence or public disorder. Vombatkere kept it in abeyance and stayed proceedings.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the two decisions and invents a revival. Option C confuses the 2023 Commission safeguard with the Court's judgment. Option D swaps the two holdings.
questions.clat_trap: Reversal of two cases is a standard CLAT trap; each wrong option attaches the right holding to the wrong case.
questions.language_trick: 'abeyance' is not 'struck down'; a stay is not an invalidation.

questions.question: A trial court imposes the death sentence for a brutal murder relying only on the manner of the crime and without examining the offender's background. On the passage, the sentence is vulnerable because

options.A: Machhi Singh requires every death sentence to be confirmed by the Supreme Court within one year of the trial verdict
options.B: the 262nd Report bars capital punishment for every offence other than terrorism-related offences, and courts must follow it
options.C: the court must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances and also collect material on mitigation before it sentences
options.D: section 354(3) permits a death sentence only after the Governor has recommended it in a written report to the court

questions.explanation: Bachan Singh requires a balance of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, and Manoj stresses collecting mitigation material.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A converts a non-binding report into a bar. Option B invents a gubernatorial recommendation. Option D invents a one-year confirmation rule.
questions.clat_trap: The 262nd Report is the tempting option because it appears in the passage, but its status is only persuasive.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which of the following inferences is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: Shatrughan Chauhan held that a death sentence becomes unconstitutional the moment a mercy petition is filed by the convict
options.B: The 279th Report proposed retaining section 124A after the Court had already suspended the section's operation
options.C: Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan reflects judicial restraint on a subject where Parliament was thought better placed to legislate
options.D: Bachan Singh allows the death penalty only where special reasons are recorded and the case is of the rarest kind

questions.explanation: Shatrughan Chauhan treats only inordinate and unexplained delay as a ground for commutation. Filing a mercy petition does not make a sentence unconstitutional.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D follow from the passage: the Court declined to legislate, the 2023 Report followed the 2022 abeyance, and the special-reasons requirement flows from section 354(3).
questions.clat_trap: The 'NOT supported' stem makes the false statement the correct answer, and the false statement is a distorted version of a real holding.
questions.language_trick: 'the moment' turns a conditional rule into an absolute one.

passages.title: The Verma Committee, Sexual Offence Reforms and Vishaka
passages.passage: Within a month of the December 2012 Delhi gang rape, a three-member committee headed by Justice J.S. Verma, a former Chief Justice, submitted its report after receiving about eighty thousand suggestions. It recommended widening the definition of rape, deleting the marital-rape exception, creating offences of stalking, voyeurism and acid attack, and fixing command responsibility on police. It did not recommend the death penalty; it proposed enhanced punishment up to imprisonment for life, meaning the remainder of the convict's natural life. The Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013, which followed an Ordinance, inserted sections 354A to 354D, 326A and 326B and sections 376A to 376E, raised the age of consent to eighteen and provided death for rape causing death or a persistent vegetative state and for repeat offenders. The marital-rape exception (Exception 2 to section 375) was retained. After the Kathua and Unnao cases, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2018 prescribed a minimum of ten years for rape, death for rape of a girl below twelve, and barred anticipatory bail in specified cases. In Independent Thought v Union of India (2017), the Court read down Exception 2 so that sexual intercourse with a wife aged between fifteen and eighteen is rape. Justice Verma had earlier headed the Bench in Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997), which laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace, drawing on Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 and the CEDAW in the absence of legislation. Parliament later enacted the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, requiring Internal Complaints Committees. In Aureliano Fernandes v State of Goa (2023) the Court issued directions to ensure implementation of the Act. A challenge to the marital-rape exception remains pending before the Supreme Court (verify current status).

questions.question: On the death penalty, the position of the Verma Committee was that

options.A: it recommended death only for rape of girls below twelve, which the 2018 Act then enacted into the Penal Code
options.B: it left the question to the courts and made no recommendation at all on the quantum of punishment
options.C: it recommended death for every rape conviction, a view the 2013 Act then accepted in full without any change
options.D: it favoured enhanced imprisonment up to life, meaning the natural life, rather than capital punishment

questions.explanation: The Committee proposed enhanced imprisonment and did not recommend death. Parliament nevertheless provided death in some cases in 2013.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the Committee's position. Option B attributes the 2018 Act's rule to the Committee. Option C says the Committee was silent although the passage records a proposal.
questions.clat_trap: The 2013 Act did provide death in some cases, which tempts students to assume the Committee had recommended it.
questions.language_trick: 'meaning the remainder of the convict's natural life' fixes the sense of 'life'.

questions.question: Which of the following Verma Committee recommendations was NOT accepted in the 2013 Act?

options.A: Removing the exception that protects a husband who has intercourse with his wife from the definition of rape
options.B: Creating a distinct offence of stalking covering repeated following of or contact with a woman against her wish
options.C: Creating a distinct offence of acid attack with a separate penal provision for causing and attempting it
options.D: Creating a distinct offence of voyeurism covering the watching or capture of a woman in a private act

questions.explanation: The 2013 Act inserted stalking, voyeurism and acid attack provisions but retained Exception 2 to section 375.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D were accepted: the Act inserted sections 354D, 354C and 326A and 326B respectively (as the passage lists sections 354A to 354D, 326A and 326B).
questions.clat_trap: Negative stem: the answer is the recommendation that failed, and the three decoys are all accepted ones.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A man has intercourse without consent with his wife, who is sixteen. On the passage, he

options.A: commits rape only if she is below fifteen, since the Court read the exception down to that age alone
options.B: commits rape, because the exception was read down for wives aged between fifteen and eighteen
options.C: commits rape only if the marriage is shown to be void, because the exception covers valid marriages only
options.D: is protected by the exception, since the 2013 Act retained it and no court has ever read it down

questions.explanation: Independent Thought read down Exception 2 so that intercourse with a wife aged fifteen to eighteen is rape.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores the 2017 decision. Option C confuses the lower and upper limits. Option D adds a requirement about a void marriage.
questions.clat_trap: The retention of the exception in 2013 is a trap that makes the wrong options look correct unless the 2017 reading down is remembered.
questions.language_trick: 'read down' is not 'struck down'; the exception survives for wives of eighteen and above.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Vishaka guidelines could operate as law although no statute then existed on workplace sexual harassment. Reason (R): The Court drew on Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 and on the CEDAW to fill the legislative gap.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The guidelines held the field until Parliament acted in 2013. The Court's reliance on fundamental rights and the Convention is the reason they could do so.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R explains how the Court could issue binding guidelines in the absence of legislation, so it explains A.
questions.clat_trap: A reading that treats the Court as lawmaking tempts students to deny A. The passage states the basis for the guidelines.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A man has consensual intercourse with a seventeen-year-old girl who is not his wife, after the 2013 Act. On the passage, the intercourse is

options.A: not rape, because the Verma Committee had recommended retaining sixteen as the age of consent
options.B: rape only if she was below fifteen, the age fixed by Independent Thought for the wife's exception
options.C: rape, because the 2013 Act raised the age of consent to eighteen years for every girl
options.D: not rape, because the consent of a girl above sixteen is valid under the 2013 Act

questions.explanation: The passage says the 2013 Act raised the age of consent to eighteen. The fifteen-to-eighteen reading down concerns wives only.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the old age. Option B confuses the wife's exception with the general age of consent. Option D invents a Committee recommendation.
questions.clat_trap: Independent Thought concerns wives, so using it for a girl who is not a wife is the trap.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Consider: I. Independent Thought struck down Exception 2 to section 375 in its entirety. II. The 2013 Act provided death for repeat offenders of rape. III. The 2018 Act provided death for rape of a girl below twelve. IV. The Verma Committee recommended deleting the marital-rape exception. Which are correct?

options.A: I, II, III and IV only
options.B: II, III and IV only
options.C: I, III and IV only
options.D: I, II and IV only

questions.explanation: Statement I is wrong because the exception was read down for wives aged fifteen to eighteen, not struck down. Statements II, III and IV match the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A includes statement I and omits III. Option C omits the Committee's recommendation. Option D includes statement I and omits II.
questions.clat_trap: A statement-combination with one subtle false statement: 'struck down in its entirety' replaces 'read down'.
questions.language_trick: 'in its entirety' makes statement I false.

passages.title: The Malimath Committee, Witness Protection and Fair Trial
passages.passage: The Committee on Reforms of Criminal Justice System, chaired by Justice V.S. Malimath (2003), proposed a shift towards inquisitorial features. It recommended that the standard of proof in criminal trials move from 'beyond reasonable doubt' to 'clear and convincing' proof, that an adverse inference be drawn from the accused's silence, that confessions to a Superintendent of Police be admissible, that investigation be separated from law and order, that a Director of Prosecution be created, and that a victim compensation scheme and witness protection be established. None of these was accepted wholesale. The Supreme Court had already shaped the field. In Nandini Satpathy v P.L. Dani (1978) it held that the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) extends to the stage of investigation and is not confined to the courtroom. In Hussainara Khatoon (1979) it read speedy trial into Article 21. In Zahira Habibulla Sheikh (the Best Bakery case, 2004), it held that a fair trial includes protection of witnesses, since a trial vitiated by hostile or intimidated witnesses is no trial. Later, in Mahender Chawla v Union of India (2018), the Court approved the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 and declared it to be law under Articles 141 and 142 until Parliament legislates. Section 357A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, inserted in 2008, requires every State to prepare a victim compensation scheme, building on earlier directions in Delhi Domestic Working Women's Forum (1995). The Law Commission's 198th Report on witness identity protection also contributed to the debate. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita provides for witness protection schemes (verify the section). The Malimath recommendations are, as a matter of law, only recommendations.

questions.question: The Malimath Committee's proposal on the standard of proof was

options.A: to replace proof beyond reasonable doubt with 'clear and convincing' proof, which was not adopted
options.B: to adopt the civil standard of preponderance of probabilities, which Parliament enacted in 2008 along with section 357A
options.C: to lower the standard only for offences under special statutes, which the Court approved in Zahira Habibulla Sheikh
options.D: to retain proof beyond reasonable doubt but shift the burden of proving innocence on the accused, which the Court adopted

questions.explanation: The passage records the proposal and that none of the proposals was accepted wholesale.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B invents a burden shift and a judicial adoption. Option C gives a different standard and an enactment that did not occur. Option D invents a special-statute limit and a judicial approval.
questions.clat_trap: The options mix real names from the passage with invented outcomes.
questions.language_trick: 'clear and convincing' is a middle standard, different from preponderance.

questions.question: Mahender Chawla v Union of India is significant because it

options.A: held that witness protection flows only from section 357A and needs no separate scheme of any kind
options.B: struck down the Scheme as vague and directed the Law Commission to draft a fresh scheme within a year
options.C: gave the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 the force of law under Articles 141 and 142 until Parliament legislates
options.D: established speedy trial as part of Article 21 for the first time in an Indian court of law, in an appeal against conviction

questions.explanation: The Court approved the Scheme and declared it law until Parliament legislates.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses witness protection with victim compensation. Option B says the Scheme was struck down. Option D attributes Hussainara Khatoon's holding to Mahender Chawla.
questions.clat_trap: Case-name confusion: the speedy trial holding belongs to Hussainara Khatoon.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A person named as accused in an FIR is questioned by the police during investigation. On the passage, he

options.A: may invoke it only if a Magistrate has first recorded his statement and then formally framed a charge against him
options.B: may invoke Article 20(3), since the protection extends beyond the courtroom to the stage of investigation
options.C: may invoke it only against a Superintendent of Police, since confessions to that officer are admissible
options.D: cannot invoke it, because the protection begins only when the trial commences before a court of law

questions.explanation: Nandini Satpathy extended the right against self-incrimination to the investigation stage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confines the right to trial. Option C adds a Magistrate and charge requirement. Option D wrongly treats the Malimath proposal on confessions to a Superintendent of Police as law.
questions.clat_trap: The Malimath proposal on confessions appears in the passage and tempts students to treat it as law.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Which statement about Hussainara Khatoon and Zahira Habibulla Sheikh is supported by the passage?

options.A: Hussainara dealt with witness protection and Zahira dealt with speedy trial under Article 21
options.B: Both were decided after the Malimath Committee and relied on its report in their reasoning on fair trial
options.C: Both held that a fair trial depends chiefly on the standard of proof, prompting the Malimath proposal
options.D: Hussainara grounded speedy trial in Article 21; Zahira linked a fair trial to witness protection

questions.explanation: The passage assigns speedy trial to Hussainara (1979) and witness protection to Zahira (2004).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a common holding on standard of proof. Option B swaps the subjects. Option C reverses chronology: Hussainara (1979) and Zahira (2004) predate the 2003 report only in part, and Zahira did not rely on it.
questions.clat_trap: Reversal of two cases' subjects is a standard trap.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Because the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 operates as law, Parliament is barred from enacting a statutory witness protection regime. Reason (R): The Court declared the Scheme to be law only until Parliament legislates.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because the Scheme operates only until Parliament legislates. R is true and states precisely that limit.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A reads a temporary judicial arrangement as a bar on legislation. R correctly states that the arrangement is interim.
questions.clat_trap: The phrase 'operates as law' tempts students to assume a permanent and exclusive regime.
questions.language_trick: 'only until' in R defeats A.

questions.question: Which is the most accurate description of the legal status of the Malimath recommendations on the passage?

options.A: They are binding directions, because the Committee was appointed by the Union Government after consultation
options.B: They are persuasive proposals only, some of whose themes later appeared in judicial schemes and statutory provisions
options.C: They are void, because inquisitorial features cannot be reconciled with Articles 20(3) and 21 of the Constitution of India
options.D: They are binding only to the extent the Court cited them in Mahender Chawla for the Witness Protection Scheme

questions.explanation: The passage says the recommendations are only recommendations as a matter of law, although victim compensation and witness protection themes found expression elsewhere.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns appointment into binding force. Option C invents a citation by the Court in Mahender Chawla. Option D says they are void, which the passage does not say.
questions.clat_trap: 'only to the extent' options sound careful, but the passage never links Mahender Chawla to the Committee.
questions.language_trick: 'themes' not 'proposals': themes appeared, the specific proposals were not adopted.

passages.title: Police and Vigilance Reform: Commissions and Court Directions
passages.passage: Police and vigilance reform in India has proceeded through commissions and judicial directions. The National Police Commission (1977-81) submitted eight reports and drafted a Model Police Act to replace the Police Act of 1861; the Vohra Committee (1993) examined the nexus between criminals, politicians and bureaucrats; and the Soli Sorabjee Committee (2005) produced the Model Police Act, 2006. In Vineet Narain (1997-98), the Court sought to insulate the CBI and the Central Vigilance Commission from executive control, and Parliament gave the CVC statutory status through the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003. In Subramanian Swamy v Director, CBI (2014), a five-judge Bench struck down section 6A of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, which required prior approval for investigating senior officials, as violating Article 14. In Prakash Singh v Union of India (2006), the Court issued seven directions, including State Security Commissions, a fixed two-year tenure for the Director General of Police, separation of investigation from law and order, a Police Establishment Board and Police Complaints Authorities. In Lalita Kumari v Government of Uttar Pradesh (2013), a five-judge Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence, though a preliminary inquiry, to be completed within seven days, is allowed in categories such as matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence and corruption cases and cases of delay in reporting. In D.K. Basu (1997), guidelines on arrest and detention were laid down, and in Arnesh Kumar (2014) the Court insisted on a notice of appearance under section 41A for offences punishable up to seven years. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 followed the First Administrative Reforms Commission's proposal of 1966.

questions.question: Which of the following is a direction in Prakash Singh (2006)?

options.A: Prior executive approval before investigating any officer of the rank of Joint Secretary and above
options.B: Transfer of all State investigations to the CBI if they remain pending beyond sixty days from the FIR
options.C: A fixed minimum tenure of two years for the Director General of Police
options.D: A requirement that every FIR be reviewed by the Central Vigilance Commission before investigation begins

questions.explanation: The passage lists State Security Commissions, a fixed two-year tenure for the DGP, separation of investigation from law and order, a Police Establishment Board and Police Complaints Authorities.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a CVC role. Option B describes the approval regime in section 6A that was struck down in a different case. Option D invents a sixty-day transfer rule.
questions.clat_trap: Option 2 reproduces the struck-down section 6A and tempts a student who merges the two cases.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Model Police Act, 2006 is binding on all the States. Reason (R): The Soli Sorabjee Committee drafted the Model Police Act, 2006.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false because a model Act is a draft for States to adopt. R is true, as the passage states that the Soli Sorabjee Committee produced it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is accurate but does not make the draft binding.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'Model' signals a template. Students confuse a committee draft with an enacted law.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Section 6A of the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act was struck down in Subramanian Swamy because

options.A: it vested the investigation power in the CVC rather than the CBI, contravening the scheme of the CVC Act, 2003 as enacted
options.B: it created an unreasonable classification by shielding senior officials from investigation, contrary to Article 14
options.C: it required approval from a court, which the Court held to be an executive function under Article 50
options.D: it conflicted with Prakash Singh's direction on a fixed tenure for the Director General of Police

questions.explanation: The passage records that a five-judge Bench struck the section down as violating Article 14.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents a conflict with the CVC Act. Option C wrongly says approval came from a court. Option D invents a conflict with Prakash Singh.
questions.clat_trap: Several case names in the passage make cross-case confusion easy.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A complaint of corruption is received and the police hold a preliminary inquiry for twenty days before deciding whether to register an FIR. On the passage, the inquiry is

options.A: permissible in corruption cases, but it was required to be completed within seven days of the complaint
options.B: permissible without any time limit so long as it is conducted in good faith by a senior officer
options.C: impermissible in corruption cases, since registration of the FIR is mandatory in every cognizable offence
options.D: valid, because the seven-day limit applies only to matrimonial cases in the listed categories

questions.explanation: Lalita Kumari allows a preliminary inquiry in specified categories, including corruption, but it is to be completed within seven days.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the exception for listed categories. Option C drops the seven-day limit. Option D restricts the limit to one category.
questions.clat_trap: Mandatory registration is the general rule, and the question tests the exception and its limit together.
questions.language_trick: 'mandatory' is subject to the listed categories.

questions.question: Arnesh Kumar (2014) is best read as requiring that, for offences punishable up to seven years,

options.A: the accused be released on bail by the police station itself without any intervention of a court
options.B: the preliminary inquiry be completed within seven days from the receipt of the complaint
options.C: the police issue a notice of appearance under section 41A instead of arresting mechanically
options.D: the police must obtain a Magistrate's prior approval before registering the FIR in each such case

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court insisted on a notice of appearance under section 41A for offences punishable up to seven years.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A invents prior approval. Option B invents a station-level bail rule. Option D confuses the seven-year punishment limit with the seven-day inquiry limit.
questions.clat_trap: Two different 'seven's appear in the passage, which is a deliberate trap.
questions.language_trick: 'seven years' (punishment) is not 'seven days' (inquiry).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct on the passage?

options.A: Arnesh Kumar dispensed with section 41A notices for offences punishable up to seven years
options.B: D.K. Basu laid down arrest guidelines about seventeen years before Arnesh Kumar was decided
options.C: Lalita Kumari's list of cases where a preliminary inquiry is allowed includes cases of delay in reporting
options.D: Subramanian Swamy and Lalita Kumari were each decided by a five-judge Bench of the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: Arnesh Kumar insisted on section 41A notices, so the statement in the correct option reverses its effect.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are accurate: delay in reporting is listed, both were five-judge Benches, and 1997 to 2014 is seventeen years.
questions.clat_trap: Negative stem; the false statement reverses a real holding.
questions.language_trick: 'dispensed with' reverses 'insisted on'.

passages.title: Electoral Reform Committees and the Supreme Court
passages.passage: Electoral reform in India has been driven by committees and by the Supreme Court. The Tarkunde Committee (1975), the Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) and the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998, on partial State funding of elections) examined candidate disclosure, appointments to the Election Commission and election funding, while the Vohra Committee (1993) exposed the criminal-politician nexus. In Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms (2002), the Court held that voters have a right to know the criminal, financial and educational antecedents of candidates under Article 19(1)(a). In Lily Thomas v Union of India (2013), it struck down section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, which had allowed convicted legislators to continue pending appeal, so that disqualification follows conviction. In Public Interest Foundation (2018), a five-judge Bench declined to add disqualification on mere framing of charges, leaving the matter to Parliament, but directed candidates to declare criminal cases widely. In Anoop Baranwal v Union of India (2023), a five-judge Bench held that appointments of Election Commissioners under Article 324(2) be made by a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice until Parliament legislates; the 2023 Act substituted a Union Cabinet Minister for the Chief Justice, and a challenge to it is pending (verify current status). In ADR v Union of India (15 February 2024), a five-judge Bench unanimously struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme and the connected amendments to the Representation of the People Act, the Companies Act and the Income Tax Act, holding that they violated Article 19(1)(a) by denying voters information and enabling quid pro quo. The Sixty-first Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from twenty-one to eighteen by amending Article 326.

questions.question: Lily Thomas v Union of India (2013) is best described as holding that

options.A: disqualification arises only on the framing of charges, which the Court added as a new ground
options.B: section 8(4) was valid, and a convicted legislator may continue for three months to file an appeal
options.C: section 8(4) was unconstitutional, so that a convicted legislator is disqualified on conviction
options.D: disqualification arises only after the final appeal has been decided by the Supreme Court itself

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court struck down section 8(4), so disqualification follows conviction.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the pre-2013 position. Option B gives the proposal the Court declined to adopt in 2018. Option D invents a final-appeal rule.
questions.clat_trap: Two decisions on disqualification (2013 and 2018) are easy to mix up.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Sixty-first Amendment (1988) amended

options.A: Article 19(1)(a) to include an express fundamental right to vote in elections
options.B: Article 324 to enlarge the Election Commission's power over appointments and removals of Commissioners
options.C: Article 102 to disqualify persons convicted of an offence from membership of Parliament
options.D: Article 326 so as to lower the voting age for elections to the House of the People and State Assemblies from twenty-one to eighteen years

questions.explanation: The passage states the amendment amended Article 326 and the age was lowered from twenty-one to eighteen.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses Article 324 with 326. Option B invents a fundamental right to vote. Option C confuses disqualification with voter age.
questions.clat_trap: Several election-related articles appear in the passage, so matching the amendment to the right article is the test.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A vacancy arises today for the post of Election Commissioner. On the passage, the selection committee under the 2023 Act

options.A: consists of the Prime Minister alone, since Article 324(2) vests the power of appointment in the President
options.B: consists of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice, as the 2023 Act left Anoop Baranwal untouched
options.C: includes a Union Cabinet Minister in place of the Chief Justice, a design that is under challenge
options.D: is chosen by the Election Commission itself, following the Dinesh Goswami Committee's proposal

questions.explanation: Anoop Baranwal's committee was interim, operating until Parliament legislates. The 2023 Act substituted a Union Cabinet Minister for the Chief Justice.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A describes the interim arrangement as still in force. Option B ignores any committee. Option D invents a self-selection rule.
questions.clat_trap: The Court's committee was explicitly interim, so the later Act is not a contradiction of the judgment per se.
questions.language_trick: 'until Parliament legislates' is the key phrase.

questions.question: Public Interest Foundation (2018) differs from Lily Thomas (2013) in that

options.A: it struck down disqualification on framing of charges, whereas Lily Thomas declined to disturb Parliament's existing scheme under the Representation of the People Act
options.B: it left to Parliament the question of disqualification on framing of charges, whereas Lily Thomas struck down a statutory provision
options.C: it held that voters have a right to know candidates' antecedents, whereas Lily Thomas dealt with electoral bonds
options.D: it dealt with appointment of Election Commissioners, whereas Lily Thomas dealt with candidates' disclosure of antecedents

questions.explanation: Public Interest Foundation declined to add a disqualification ground and left it to Parliament, while Lily Thomas struck down section 8(4).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the two outcomes. Option C and Option D attach subjects to the wrong cases.
questions.clat_trap: A reversal of outcome combined with the same subject (disqualification) makes the first wrong option tempting.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Electoral Bond Scheme was struck down only because it was introduced through amendments to three different statutes. Reason (R): The Court held that the Scheme violated the voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a).

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false, because the passage gives Article 19(1)(a) and the quid pro quo concern as the ground, not the number of statutes. R is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: 'only because' narrows the ground wrongly. R states the actual ground.
questions.clat_trap: The passage mentions three statutes, which tempts a student to treat that fact as the reason.
questions.language_trick: 'only because' is the trap word.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT on the passage?

options.A: The Anoop Baranwal arrangement was to operate until Parliament legislates on the appointments
options.B: In 2018 the Bench left the addition of a disqualification ground to Parliament
options.C: The 2024 electoral bonds decision was unanimous and was delivered by a five-judge Bench
options.D: The Indrajit Gupta Committee recommended full State funding of elections to all legislatures, leaving no role for party or private contributions

questions.explanation: The passage says the Indrajit Gupta Committee examined partial State funding, not full State funding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option C are accurate statements.
questions.clat_trap: Negative stem; the false option changes a single adjective.
questions.language_trick: 'partial' becomes 'full'.

passages.title: Sarkaria, Finance Commissions and the Balance of Indian Federalism
passages.passage: The framers created a Union with a strong Centre, and later commissions have examined how that balance works in practice. The Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) recommended that Article 356 be used sparingly and only as a last resort, that the Inter-State Council contemplated by Article 263 be set up on a permanent basis, and that Governors be appointed after consultation with the Chief Minister. The Inter-State Council was constituted in 1990 by a Presidential order; it is a forum to discuss disputes and policy, and it cannot adjudicate. Zonal Councils, by contrast, are statutory bodies created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. The Punchhi Commission (2007-10) later revisited the same questions. The Finance Commission under Article 280 is constituted every five years to recommend how the net proceeds of taxes are to be shared between the Union and the States and the principles that govern grants-in-aid. Its recommendations are not binding, but Article 281 requires them to be laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken. The 73rd and 74th Amendments inserted Articles 243I and 243Y, requiring each State to constitute its own Finance Commission, and added to the Union Commission's task the recommendation of measures to supplement the resources of panchayats and municipalities. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine-judge Bench held that federalism is a basic feature of the Constitution and that a proclamation under Article 356 is justiciable, since the Centre must have relevant material for it. Inter-State river disputes are dealt with under Article 262, which allows Parliament to bar the jurisdiction of courts, and the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 contains such a bar. In 2018, in the Cauvery dispute, the Supreme Court heard appeals against the Tribunal's award and modified the allocation, observing that river water is a national asset and no State can claim exclusive ownership of it.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Inter-State Council as presented in the passage?

options.A: A body set up under Article 263 by a Presidential order, whose role is to discuss and advise and not to adjudicate
options.B: A statutory body created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, whose recommendations bind the States concerned
options.C: A constitutional tribunal under Article 262 that decides inter-State river disputes finally
options.D: A regional forum of the Zonal Council type, whose decisions on disputes between States are enforceable by the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: The passage says the Council was constituted in 1990 by a Presidential order under the power contemplated in Article 263 and that it cannot adjudicate.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B describes Zonal Councils, which are statutory, and not the Inter-State Council. Option C confuses Article 263 with Article 262. Option D treats an advisory forum as an enforcing one.
questions.clat_trap: Three bodies with similar-sounding names are placed side by side, and each wrong option borrows a true feature of another body.
questions.language_trick: 'adjudicate' versus 'discuss': the verb in the stem decides which institution is meant.

questions.question: The Union accepts part of a Finance Commission's recommendations and rejects the rest. On the passage, the constitutionally correct position is that

options.A: the rejection is void, since the President is bound to give effect to what the Commission recommends under Article 280
options.B: the rejection is valid only if the Inter-State Council has first approved it under Article 263
options.C: the rejection is valid as the recommendations are not binding, but the report must still be laid before Parliament
options.D: the rejection is valid, and since the Government chose not to implement the report it need not be laid before Parliament at all

questions.explanation: Article 280 recommendations are advisory, but Article 281 imposes the duty to lay the report and the memorandum before Parliament.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a recommendation into a command. Option B correctly says the rejection is valid but wrongly removes the laying requirement. Option D imports an approval step that does not exist.
questions.clat_trap: One option is half right: the rejection is valid, but the duty to lay is dropped. Half-correct options are the commonest CLAT trap.
questions.language_trick: 'not binding' and 'must be laid' operate at different levels: one is about the effect of the report, the other about a procedural duty.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: The 73rd and 74th Amendments require States to constitute their own Finance Commissions
options.B: Zonal Councils are constitutional bodies created under Article 263 alongside the Inter-State Council
options.C: A proclamation under Article 356 can be tested in court for the existence of relevant material
options.D: The Sarkaria Commission recommended that the Inter-State Council be established on a permanent basis

questions.explanation: The passage describes Zonal Councils as statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, not constitutional bodies.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D are each stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A negatively framed stem makes the false statement the correct choice, and the three true statements are all drawn closely from the text.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT supported' asks for the odd one out. A reader who looks for the true statement marks the wrong option.

questions.question: The holding in Bommai that a proclamation under Article 356 is justiciable means that

options.A: courts may substitute their own view of the political wisdom of imposing the proclamation
options.B: the President's satisfaction is final, as review is barred by the immunity attached to advice given to the President
options.C: courts may examine whether relevant material existed, so the Centre's satisfaction is not immune
options.D: review is possible only after the Assembly has been dissolved and the elections have been held

questions.explanation: Justiciability in Bommai means courts can test the existence of relevant material. It does not mean courts replace the executive's political judgment.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the position that Bommai rejected. Option B overstates review into a merits inquiry. Option D invents a timing limit.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is moderate in tone, while two wrong options push to opposite extremes, one of no review and one of full review.
questions.language_trick: 'relevant material' is a limited standard of review, which is different from reviewing 'wisdom'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Supreme Court could not have heard the Cauvery appeals in 2018, since Article 262 allows Parliament to bar the jurisdiction of courts over inter-State river disputes. Reason (R): In 2018 the Supreme Court heard appeals against the Tribunal's award and modified the allocation.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The passage records that the Court heard the appeals and modified the allocation, so R is true. A is false because the existence of a power to oust jurisdiction does not mean that the Court could not hear the appeals.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A confuses a power Parliament may use with the actual outcome; R is a plain statement from the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The fact that Article 262 permits a bar tempts a reader to treat A as true.
questions.language_trick: 'could not have heard' is a categorical claim that the passage contradicts.

questions.question: A State argues that the Sarkaria Commission recommended consultation with the Chief Minister before a Governor is appointed, and that a Governor appointed without such consultation therefore holds office unconstitutionally. On the passage, the argument

options.A: fails, as a Commission's recommendation lacks the force of law and the passage records no bar to appointment without consultation
options.B: fails only because Governors are appointed under Article 356, which does not require consultation
options.C: succeeds, because Bommai made federalism a basic feature of the Constitution, so every recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission has become mandatory on the Union
options.D: succeeds, because the Commission's recommendations were adopted through the Inter-State Council under Article 263

questions.explanation: A commission's report persuades but does not bind. Neither the Inter-State Council nor Bommai converts a recommendation into a constitutional requirement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B wrongly presumes adoption. Option C stretches a basic-feature holding into binding force for every recommendation. Option D misdescribes the source of Governors' appointment.
questions.clat_trap: Basic-structure language sounds weighty, which tempts a reader to treat every federal recommendation as constitutionally mandatory.
questions.language_trick: 'therefore holds office unconstitutionally' is the leap from recommendation to illegality.

passages.title: From Balwant Rai Mehta to the 73rd and 74th Amendments: Local Bodies and Reservation
passages.passage: Democratic decentralisation was studied by the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957), which recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system, and by the Ashok Mehta Committee (1977), which favoured a two-tier structure with the district as the unit. The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) urged constitutional recognition of local bodies. The 73rd Amendment (1992) inserted Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule, and the 74th Amendment inserted Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule for municipalities. A Panchayat has a five-year term; elections must be held before the term ends or, if it is dissolved, within six months; one-third of seats are reserved for women, and seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are reserved in proportion to their population. Article 243-O bars courts from interfering in electoral matters of Panchayats, while Article 243M exempts Scheduled Areas from Part IX unless Parliament extends it. In Kishansing Tomar v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad (2006), the Supreme Court stressed that the State Election Commission must hold local elections on time and that the State cannot postpone them at will. In K. Krishna Murthy v. Union of India (2010), a Constitution Bench upheld the reservations in local bodies under Articles 243D(6) and 243T(6) as a distinct category of political reservation, but held that the reasoning cannot be carried over to Parliament and the State Legislatures. In Vikas Kishanrao Gawali v. State of Maharashtra (2021), the Court set aside an ordinance that sought to continue OBC reservation in local bodies, holding that the State must satisfy a triple test: set up a dedicated commission to conduct an empirical inquiry, specify the proportion of reservation local body-wise on that basis, and ensure that the total of SC, ST and OBC reservations does not exceed fifty per cent.

questions.question: Which pairing of committee and recommendation is accurate on the passage?

options.A: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee: constitutional recognition for local bodies
options.B: Ashok Mehta Committee: a two-tier structure with the district as the unit
options.C: L.M. Singhvi Committee: a three-tier Panchayati Raj system
options.D: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee: a two-tier structure with the district as the unit

questions.explanation: The Ashok Mehta Committee favoured two tiers with the district as the unit. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended three tiers, and the Singhvi Committee urged constitutional recognition.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives the Singhvi recommendation to Balwant Rai Mehta. Option C gives Balwant Rai Mehta's recommendation to Singhvi. Option D gives Ashok Mehta's recommendation to Balwant Rai Mehta.
questions.clat_trap: All options use real committees and real recommendations, so only the pairing is wrong.
questions.language_trick: 'pairing' tells you to match, not just to recognise a true fact.

questions.question: A State dissolves a Panchayat in the third year of its term and proposes to hold fresh elections eleven months later. On the passage, the proposal

options.A: breaches the rule that elections must be held within six months of dissolution
options.B: is valid, because the State Election Commission may fix any date within the remaining term of the dissolved body
options.C: breaches the rule only if the dissolved Panchayat was situated in a Scheduled Area
options.D: is valid, because Article 243-O allows a State to defer elections where it has itself dissolved the body

questions.explanation: The passage states that after dissolution elections must be held within six months. Eleven months exceeds that period.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the six-month limit. Option C misreads Article 243-O, which bars court interference in electoral matters and does not permit deferral. Option D reverses the position on Scheduled Areas, which are outside Part IX unless Parliament extends it.
questions.clat_trap: Article 243-O sounds like a shield for the State, but it concerns the courts, not the timing of elections.
questions.language_trick: 'within six months' is a fixed outer limit and not a guideline.

questions.question: The reasoning in Krishna Murthy, as described in the passage, is best summarised as saying that

options.A: reservation in local bodies is valid only if the total exceeds fifty per cent, to account for political backwardness
options.B: OBC reservation in local bodies is unconstitutional because political backwardness is not a recognised criterion
options.C: local body reservation rests on a distinct footing and cannot be assumed to justify similar reservation for OBCs in Parliament and the State Legislatures
options.D: the reasoning for local body reservation extends equally to Parliament and the State Legislatures through Article 15(4)

questions.explanation: The Court upheld local body reservations as a political reservation but refused to carry the reasoning to Legislatures.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the opposite of the holding. Option B states the extension the Court declined. Option D invents a minimum that no part of the passage supports.
questions.clat_trap: The right answer keeps both halves: upheld in local bodies, not extended upward.
questions.language_trick: 'cannot be assumed' marks a limit on reasoning rather than a prohibition.

questions.question: A State has a commission's report giving the State-wide OBC population, but no local body-wise data. It fixes a uniform 27 per cent OBC quota for every local body, so that SC, ST and OBC reservations together stay at 40 per cent. On the passage, the quota

options.A: fails the triple test only because the total of the reservations exceeds fifty per cent of seats
options.B: satisfies the triple test, since a dedicated commission has already been constituted and has reported
options.C: fails the triple test, since the proportion must be set local body-wise on empirical inquiry
options.D: satisfies the triple test, since the combined total remains below the fifty per cent ceiling

questions.explanation: The triple test has three limbs, and the second requires local body-wise proportions drawn from the empirical inquiry. A uniform figure fails it even though the other two limbs may be met.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B each satisfy one limb and ignore the rest. Option D cites the cap, which this quota does not breach.
questions.clat_trap: Two of the three limbs appear to be met, and this tempts a reader to treat the test as satisfied.
questions.language_trick: 'local body-wise' is the specific words of the second limb.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated or implied by the passage?

options.A: The 74th Amendment inserted a Schedule for municipalities
options.B: Part IX applies automatically to Scheduled Areas without any further action by Parliament
options.C: One-third of Panchayat seats are reserved for women
options.D: The State Election Commission is expected to hold local elections on time

questions.explanation: Article 243M exempts Scheduled Areas from Part IX unless Parliament extends it, so the stated proposition is false.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D are each supported by the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The true statements are plain, while the false one tests the exemption for Scheduled Areas.
questions.language_trick: 'automatically' and 'without any further action' conflict with 'unless Parliament extends it'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A State may lawfully postpone local body elections indefinitely while it completes the empirical inquiry needed for OBC reservation. Reason (R): Article 243-O bars courts from interfering in electoral matters of Panchayats.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is false, because Kishansing Tomar holds that the State cannot postpone elections at will and the triple test does not suspend the duty to hold them on time. R correctly states Article 243-O but does not justify postponement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R is a true statement about the bar in Article 243-O, which relates to interference by courts in electoral matters and does not license the State to delay elections.
questions.clat_trap: A true Reason beside a false Assertion tempts the reader to link them, since Article 243-O seems to protect State action from the courts.
questions.language_trick: 'indefinitely' makes A an overstatement.

passages.title: Bhuria Committee, PESA and the Rights of Scheduled Area Communities
passages.passage: Tribal self-governance has been examined by the Dhebar Commission (1961) and the Bhuria Committee (1995). The latter's recommendations shaped the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), enacted under Article 243M(4)(b) to extend Part IX to Scheduled Areas with modifications. PESA gives the Gram Sabha powers over matters such as minor forest produce and the prevention of land alienation. The design rests on the Fifth Schedule, under which the Governor administers Scheduled Areas with the help of a Tribes Advisory Council. The Sixth Schedule, by contrast, creates autonomous district councils in parts of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights and gives the Gram Sabha a central role in verifying claims. In Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997), the Supreme Court held that a transfer of land in Scheduled Areas to non-tribals, including a lease by the State for mining, was invalid, and rejected the argument that the State is outside the prohibition on land alienation. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment and Forests (2013), concerning bauxite mining in the Niyamgiri hills, the Court directed that Gram Sabhas decide whether the project would affect the religious and cultural rights of the forest-dwelling Dongria Kondh community, and made the clearance of the project depend on the outcome. A committee's report does not itself change the law; the Bhuria Committee's recommendations took effect only because Parliament enacted the 1996 Act.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Fifth Schedule from the Sixth Schedule?

options.A: The Fifth Schedule applies in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, while the Sixth applies in the remaining States
options.B: Both Schedules provide for autonomous district councils, but only the Sixth also gives a role to the Gram Sabha
options.C: The Fifth Schedule creates autonomous district councils, while the Sixth has the Governor administer Scheduled Areas
options.D: The Fifth Schedule has the Governor administer Scheduled Areas with a Tribes Advisory Council, while the Sixth creates autonomous district councils in parts of four north-eastern States

questions.explanation: The passage assigns the Governor and Tribes Advisory Council to the Fifth Schedule and autonomous district councils to the Sixth, in four north-eastern States.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A swaps the two Schedules. Option B invents a shared feature. Option C assigns the Sixth Schedule States to the Fifth.
questions.clat_trap: Swapped attributes are used to catch readers who half remember the two Schedules.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: The Bhuria Committee's recommendations became operative law through

options.A: a direction of the Supreme Court in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh
options.B: the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, enacted under Article 243M(4)(b)
options.C: a constitutional amendment inserting the Fifth Schedule into the Constitution to give effect to the report
options.D: the Forest Rights Act, 2006, which Parliament passed to implement the report in full for all forest-dwelling communities

questions.explanation: The passage states that the recommendations took effect only because Parliament enacted the 1996 Act under Article 243M(4)(b).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A credits a Schedule that already existed. Option C credits a later and different statute. Option D credits a judgment that concerns land alienation, not the committee.
questions.clat_trap: Several instruments in the passage concern tribal communities, so any of them can look like the vehicle for the recommendations.
questions.language_trick: 'became operative law' asks for the legal instrument, which is different from the source of the idea.

questions.question: A State leases land in a Scheduled Area to a private company for mining, arguing that the prohibition on transfer to non-tribals binds only private persons and not the State. Applying Samatha as described, the lease is

options.A: valid, provided the Tribes Advisory Council has been consulted before the lease is executed
options.B: valid, since the prohibition addresses private persons only and the State acts for a public purpose in granting the lease
options.C: invalid, since the Court rejected the argument that the State stands outside the prohibition
options.D: invalid only if the lessee is an individual, and not if it is a company

questions.explanation: Samatha treated a State mining lease to non-tribals as a prohibited transfer and rejected the State's claimed exemption.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the argument the Court rejected. Option B adds a consultation cure that the passage does not contain. Option D invents a distinction between individuals and companies.
questions.clat_trap: The argument in the stem is actually the one the Court rejected, so a reader who finds it plausible picks the wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'rejected the argument' is a signal to reverse the stem's proposition.

questions.question: The effect of the Niyamgiri direction, as described in the passage, was that

options.A: Gram Sabhas acquired a general veto over every mining project in Scheduled Areas, whatever the rights of the community affected
options.B: the Gram Sabha's view on the community's religious and cultural rights became a decisive input on whether the project could proceed
options.C: the Court itself decided that the religious rights of the Dongria Kondh were not affected by the project, closing that question
options.D: Gram Sabhas were authorised to decide the environmental viability of the project as a whole, besides the community's cultural rights

questions.explanation: The Court asked the Gram Sabhas to decide on religious and cultural rights and made clearance depend on the outcome. It did not give a general veto or decide the facts itself.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A generalises a case-specific direction. Option C attributes a factual finding to the Court. Option D widens the Gram Sabhas' task beyond religious and cultural rights.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option is limited to the rights the Court named, while the wrong options widen or reassign the decision.
questions.language_trick: 'decisive input' is narrower than 'veto' and does not grant any power over the whole project.

questions.question: Consider the following statements. I. The Bhuria Committee's report is itself binding on the Governors of States having Scheduled Areas. II. PESA gives the Gram Sabha powers over minor forest produce and the prevention of land alienation. III. The Sixth Schedule provides for autonomous district councils in parts of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. IV. Samatha exempted State leases for mining from the prohibition on land alienation.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements II and III restate the passage. Statement I is false because a committee's report is not binding, and statement IV is false because Samatha rejected the exemption.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: I treats a recommendation as law. IV reverses the holding in Samatha.
questions.clat_trap: Each false statement uses a real name from the passage, so a reader who matches names without matching content accepts it.
questions.language_trick: 'itself binding' and 'exempted' are the words that reverse two true propositions.

questions.question: A scholar argues that, because the Bhuria Committee's report is not law, PESA has no basis in it at all. On the passage, this argument

options.A: is correct, since a statute enacted on a committee's recommendation lacks independent legal force
options.B: fails because Article 243M(4)(b) makes the reports of committees binding on Parliament whenever it legislates for Scheduled Areas
options.C: confuses where the committee's influence came from with where PESA's legal force lies: Parliament's enactment
options.D: is correct only in relation to areas under the Sixth Schedule, where PESA has no application

questions.explanation: A report can shape a law without having legal force itself. PESA is binding because Parliament enacted it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A denies independent force to an Act. Option B invents a Sixth Schedule limitation. Option D gives committee reports a binding status that Article 243M does not grant.
questions.clat_trap: The stem mixes two true points, that the report is not law and that PESA drew on it, and asks whether they conflict. They do not.
questions.language_trick: 'no basis at all' is the absolute claim that a distinction between influence and authority answers.

passages.title: Sachar, Ranganath Misra and the Evolving Doctrine of Minority Institutions
passages.passage: The Sachar Committee (2006) examined the social, economic and educational condition of Muslims in India, and the Ranganath Misra Commission (2007) recommended ten per cent reservation for Muslims and five per cent for other minorities; the recommendation was not implemented. The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions Act, 2004 created a forum to decide questions of minority status. Article 30(1) gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. In S. Azeez Basha v. Union of India (1968), a five-judge Bench held that the Aligarh Muslim University, having been established by a statute of the Central Legislature, was not 'established' by the Muslim minority and so could not claim the protection of Article 30(1). In T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka (2002), an eleven-judge Bench held that the unit for determining minority status is the State and not the nation, and that minorities may admit students of their choice subject to transparency and merit. The 93rd Amendment inserted Article 15(5), enabling special provisions for admission to educational institutions other than minority institutions. In Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal (8 November 2024), a seven-judge Bench by 4:3 overruled Azeez Basha. The majority held that an institution does not lose its minority character merely because it was incorporated by a statute; the Court must look at the origin of the institution and at who was the brain behind it. The Bench left the actual determination of the University's status to a regular Bench.

questions.question: Why did Azeez Basha deny the Aligarh Muslim University the protection of Article 30(1)?

options.A: Because Article 30(1) protects only linguistic minorities and not religious ones, so the University could not claim its benefit at all
options.B: Because incorporation by a Central statute meant that the minority had not itself established the University
options.C: Because the University admitted students from communities other than the Muslim minority, which defeated its claim to a minority character
options.D: Because minority status can be determined only by taking the whole nation as the unit and not a single State

questions.explanation: The passage says the Court treated the University as established by statute and not by the Muslim minority.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A misstates Article 30(1), which covers both kinds of minority. Option C cites a fact that the passage does not use as the reason. Option D confuses Azeez Basha with the later T.M.A. Pai question about the unit.
questions.clat_trap: Wrong options borrow real doctrinal issues, namely types of minorities, admissions and unit of determination, from other parts of the topic.
questions.language_trick: 'established' sits inside quotation marks in the passage, since the whole case turned on that word.

questions.question: A religious community forms the majority of the national population but less than half the population of a particular State. For the purposes of Article 30, on the passage's account of T.M.A. Pai,

options.A: it may claim minority status in that State, since the State and not the nation is the unit
options.B: it cannot claim minority status anywhere, since minority status is decided on the national population
options.C: it may claim minority status only if it also forms a minority in a majority of the other States
options.D: it may claim minority status only for schools and not for professional colleges

questions.explanation: T.M.A. Pai treats the State as the unit, so a community that is a numerical minority in a State can claim minority status there.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B applies the national unit that the Court rejected. Option C adds a cross-State condition. Option D adds a distinction between institutions that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: National majority status makes the community look like a non-minority, which is the intuition the holding overturns.
questions.language_trick: 'unit' is a technical term; the passage fixes it at the State.

questions.question: The ratio of Naresh Agarwal, as described in the passage, is that

options.A: the Aligarh Muslim University was declared a minority institution entitled to reserve half its seats
options.B: the 1981 position was restored for every central university established by an Act of Parliament
options.C: every institution incorporated by statute is a minority institution if its name refers to a community
options.D: statutory incorporation does not by itself defeat minority character, and the Court looks at the origin of the institution and who was its brain

questions.explanation: The majority held that incorporation by statute does not destroy minority character and set the origin-and-brain test, leaving the actual decision to a regular Bench.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a test into an automatic rule based on the name. Option B treats the University's status as already decided. Option C extends the holding to every central university.
questions.clat_trap: A headline reading of the case, that AMU won, is wrong because the status was left for a regular Bench.
questions.language_trick: 'by itself' and 'does not defeat' mark a limited holding.

questions.question: Which of the following about the Naresh Agarwal reference is accurate?

options.A: A seven-judge Bench unanimously held the University to be a minority institution and closed the matter, leaving nothing for a regular Bench
options.B: A seven-judge Bench divided 4:3 and held the University not to be a minority institution while affirming the ruling in Azeez Basha
options.C: A seven-judge Bench divided 5:2 and upheld Azeez Basha on the ground that statute-based institutions are outside Article 30(1)
options.D: A seven-judge Bench divided 4:3, overruled Azeez Basha and left the actual status of the University to a regular Bench

questions.explanation: The passage records a 4:3 decision that overruled Azeez Basha and remitted the determination.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gets the line-up and the outcome wrong. Option B reverses the vote and the effect on Azeez Basha. Option C keeps the right vote but reverses the holding.
questions.clat_trap: One wrong option keeps the correct vote of 4:3 and reverses only the outcome. Readers who recognise the vote stop reading.
questions.language_trick: 'overruled' versus 'affirmed' is the word that separates the options with the same vote.

questions.question: A State Government decides to implement ten per cent reservation for Muslims, relying on the Ranganath Misra Commission's report. On the passage, the report

options.A: validates the quota, since Article 30(1) authorises reservation for minorities in all public employment under the State
options.B: has no binding force of its own and was not implemented, so a quota would need a valid law meeting constitutional tests
options.C: binds the State Governments, since Article 15(5) requires them to act on commission reports about the welfare of minorities in the country
options.D: voids the quota, since the 93rd Amendment prohibits any reservation in favour of minorities in public employment or education

questions.explanation: A commission's recommendation is not law, and the passage says it was not implemented. Article 15(5) concerns educational institutions and carves out minority institutions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns a recommendation into a command and misuses Article 15(5). Option C overextends Article 30(1), which is about educational institutions. Option D invents a prohibition.
questions.clat_trap: Three real provisions are named in the wrong options, and each is applied to something it does not govern.
questions.language_trick: 'relying on' signals that the stem tests the legal weight of the report.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Article 15(5), as inserted by the 93rd Amendment, permits the State to reserve seats in a minority educational institution established under Article 30(1). Reason (R): Article 15(5) enables special provisions for admission to educational institutions other than minority institutions.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
