options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R correctly states the carve-out. A is therefore false, because the provision does not extend to minority institutions.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A reverses the carve-out, while R states it accurately.
questions.clat_trap: Both sentences use the same provisions, so a quick reader assumes that R supports A.
questions.language_trick: 'other than' in R is the phrase that contradicts A.

passages.title: Law Commission, Shetty Commission and Reform of the Subordinate Judiciary
passages.passage: The Law Commission's 14th Report (1958) examined the reform of judicial administration and favoured an All-India Judicial Service. The 42nd Amendment (1976) amended Article 312 to allow Parliament to create such a service for the judiciary, but provided that it cannot include any post inferior to that of a district judge. Articles 233 to 237 govern the subordinate judiciary: the Governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court, and Article 235 vests control over district courts and the courts subordinate to them in the High Court. In All India Judges' Association v. Union of India (1993), the Supreme Court directed the creation of an All-India Judicial Service. In a later round (2002) it accepted most of the recommendations of the Shetty Commission, the First National Judicial Pay Commission (1999), on pay and service conditions, and laid down a pattern for promotion. In All India Judges' Association v. Union of India (20 May 2025), the Court held that a minimum of three years' practice as an advocate is required to be eligible for the post of Civil Judge (Junior Division), applying to recruitments initiated after the order. The requirement was later reported to have been adjusted for a transitional period, and the present position should be verified. Article 233(2) separately requires seven years' practice as an advocate or pleader for direct appointment as a district judge from the Bar. In Brij Mohan Lal v. Union of India (2012), the Court dealt with fast-track courts and the need for more judges, and linked speedy justice to Article 21.

questions.question: The effect of the 42nd Amendment on Article 312 was to

options.A: extend the service to the post of Civil Judge (Junior Division) so that recruitment at entry level becomes a Union function
options.B: transfer control of subordinate courts from the High Court to the Union Government under the scheme of Article 235
options.C: authorise Parliament to create, by law supported by a Rajya Sabha resolution, an All-India Judicial Service whose posts are not inferior to district judge
options.D: require the Union to create the service within a fixed period after the Amendment came into force, as a mandatory duty

questions.explanation: The Amendment gave Parliament the power to create the service, with a floor at the district judge level.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A turns an enabling power into a duty with a deadline. Option B confuses Article 312 with Article 235. Option D contradicts the floor at district judge level.
questions.clat_trap: An enabling provision is easily mistaken for a mandatory one.
questions.language_trick: 'authorise' means a power and does not mean a command.

questions.question: A State Government wishes to take over the control of a district court from the High Court. On the passage, control over district courts and subordinate courts

options.A: vests in the High Court under Article 235, so the State cannot take it over
options.B: vests in the Governor alone, acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers
options.C: vests in the State Public Service Commission, which supervises recruitment and promotion
options.D: vests in the Supreme Court through the All-India Judicial Service under Article 312

questions.explanation: Article 235, as described, vests control in the High Court.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats appointment as if it were control. Option C misplaces control in a recruitment body. Option D invents Supreme Court control through the All-India service.
questions.clat_trap: The Governor appoints district judges, which makes the Governor look like the controlling authority.
questions.language_trick: 'appoints' and 'controls' are two different verbs in the passage.

questions.question: An advocate with five years' practice applies for direct appointment as a district judge from the Bar. On the passage, the application

options.A: meets the requirement, because five years exceeds the three-year minimum fixed in 2025
options.B: fails, because the All-India Judicial Service excludes candidates from the Bar
options.C: fails to meet Article 233(2), which requires seven years' practice, even though the three-year rule applies to Civil Judges
options.D: meets the requirement, because Article 233(2) requires only consultation with the High Court

questions.explanation: The three-year rule of 2025 concerns Civil Judge (Junior Division). Article 233(2) sets a separate seven-year requirement for district judges from the Bar.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the wrong number to the wrong post. Option B mistakes the consultation in Article 233(1) for the eligibility test. Option D invents a bar on Bar candidates.
questions.clat_trap: Two different practice requirements, three years and seven years, are set for two different posts.
questions.language_trick: 'direct appointment as a district judge' fixes the post, and with it the rule.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the Shetty Commission's recommendations on pay and service conditions

options.A: acquired operative force largely because the Court accepted most of them in 2002, not through the Commission's own authority
options.B: were binding from the start because Article 312 gives the reports of such a Commission the full force of law throughout the country
options.C: were rejected in 2002 and replaced by a pattern of promotion fixed by the Court on its own view of the service
options.D: were embodied in the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution, which gave effect to the pay structure it had proposed earlier

questions.explanation: The Commission's report did not bind of its own force. The Court's acceptance gave the recommendations operative effect.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B credits a provision that deals with the creation of the service. Option C reverses the Court's decision of 2002. Option D ties the Commission to an Amendment that predates it.
questions.clat_trap: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 comes earlier than the Commission of 1999, so the link in the third option is chronologically impossible.
questions.language_trick: 'largely because the Court accepted' places the source of force outside the Commission.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A recommendation of the Law Commission for an All-India Judicial Service could not by itself create the service. Reason (R): The 42nd Amendment amended Article 312 to authorise Parliament to create such a service.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Both statements are supported by the passage. A recommendation has no force of its own, and the power to create the service lies with Parliament under Article 312 as amended, which explains why the recommendation alone could not do it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R supplies the legal source of the power that a recommendation lacks.
questions.clat_trap: The reader may hesitate because the Amendment came after the 1958 Report, but R explains the legal source, not the sequence.
questions.language_trick: 'by itself' in A points to the missing legal source that R supplies.

questions.question: A recruitment for Civil Judge (Junior Division) was initiated in January 2025. A fresh law graduate with no practice applies after the order of 20 May 2025, and no transitional adjustment is assumed. On the passage, the three-year requirement

options.A: applies only to direct recruitment as district judge and not to Civil Judges
options.B: applies, since the order is declaratory of the law and so operates retrospectively
options.C: applies, since the candidate applied after the order was passed
options.D: does not apply to that recruitment, since the order applies to recruitments initiated after it

questions.explanation: The passage ties the rule to recruitments initiated after the order. The relevant date is the initiation of the recruitment, not the date of application.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A uses the date of application instead of the date of initiation. Option B assumes retrospective operation, which the passage rules out. Option C confuses the post.
questions.clat_trap: The date of application falls after the order, and this tempts a reader to apply the rule although the recruitment began earlier.
questions.language_trick: 'initiated after the order' fixes the relevant date.

passages.title: From the Viswanathan Committee to the Code: Insolvency Judgments and Amendments
passages.passage: The Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee chaired by T K Viswanathan (2015) recommended a single code for corporate and individual insolvency, a time-bound resolution process led by a Committee of Creditors (CoC) of financial creditors, and a specialised regulator. Its report led to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. A committee report is only a recommendation; the Code is the enactment the courts test. In Innoventive Industries v ICICI Bank (2017), the Supreme Court held that once a default is shown, the adjudicating authority must admit the application, that the moratorium under section 14 follows, and that the Code overrides inconsistent State legislation. In Swiss Ribbons v Union of India (2019), the Court upheld the Code and held that the distinction between financial creditors and operational creditors is intelligible and has a rational nexus with the object of the Code, so Article 14 is not violated. In Essar Steel India v Satish Kumar Gupta (2019), the Court held that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is not justiciable and that operational creditors are entitled to equitable, not equal, treatment. Pioneer Urban Land v Union of India (2019) upheld the 2018 amendment under which homebuyers are treated as financial creditors. In Ghanashyam Mishra v Edelweiss (2021), the Court held that once a resolution plan is approved, all claims not forming part of the plan stand extinguished. The Code was amended in 2021 to introduce pre-packaged insolvency resolution for micro, small and medium enterprises. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Bill, 2025, which proposes creditor-initiated insolvency, group insolvency and tighter timelines, was passed by the Lok Sabha in March 2026; its present status should be verified.

questions.question: Swiss Ribbons v Union of India rejected the Article 14 challenge to the Code's treatment of creditors because

options.A: Parliament may classify creditors however it wishes so long as the Committee of Creditors later consents to the classification
options.B: the Code treats every class of creditor identically and therefore involves no classification at all that Article 14 could reach
options.C: the two classes of creditors are differently situated, so the classification is intelligible and rationally connected to the Code's object
options.D: Article 14 has no application to economic legislation dealing with insolvency and the recovery of commercial debt

questions.explanation: The Court asked whether the classification was intelligible and had a rational nexus with the Code's object. Financial and operational creditors differ in the nature of their dealings with the debtor, so the test was met.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is false, because the Code does classify creditors. Option B wrongly places economic legislation outside Article 14. Option D invents a role for CoC consent in testing constitutional validity.
questions.clat_trap: A student who remembers only that the challenge failed may choose an option that states a blanket rule. The Court applied the ordinary classification test, not an exemption.
questions.language_trick: 'differently situated' and 'rational nexus' are the words of the classification test.

questions.question: On the passage, the treatment of homebuyers under the Code is that

options.A: the 2018 amendment making them financial creditors was upheld in Pioneer Urban Land, so they can sit on the CoC
options.B: they are a separate class of secured creditors whose claims rank above those of every other financial creditor in the plan
options.C: they remain operational creditors and cannot sit on the Committee of Creditors, as the Court struck down the 2018 amendment
options.D: they became financial creditors only for projects covered by the 2021 pre-packaged insolvency scheme for small enterprises

questions.explanation: Pioneer upheld the 2018 amendment. Homebuyers therefore count as financial creditors under the Code.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the outcome of Pioneer. Option C adds a ranking rule not in the passage. Option D confuses the pre-pack scheme with the homebuyer amendment.
questions.clat_trap: Dates and amendments are scattered through the passage, so options mix 2018 and 2021 events. Matching the amendment to its case is the safe route.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A State enactment declares that no proceeding for recovery may be started for two years against a distressed company that has been given a revival package. A financial creditor proves a default and files an application under the Code. On the passage, the application

options.A: must be rejected, because a financial creditor cannot file where a revival package has already been sanctioned
options.B: must be admitted on proof of default, with the moratorium following, since the Code overrides inconsistent State law
options.C: must be stayed for two years, because the State law is a specific enactment that prevails over a general central code
options.D: may be admitted only if the State government consents, since revival of distressed companies concerns State policy

questions.explanation: Innoventive holds that on proof of default admission follows and that the Code overrides inconsistent State law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A applies the maxim that a specific law prevails over a general law, which the Court did not adopt here. Option C adds a consent requirement. Option D adds a bar not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The 'specific over general' instinct is the trap. The passage gives an express rule that the Code prevails over State law.
questions.language_trick: 'overrides inconsistent State legislation' is a statement of supremacy, not of harmonisation.

questions.question: A resolution plan is approved. Later, a tax department raises a demand for an earlier period, which was never part of the plan or the claims in the process. On the passage, the demand

options.A: stands extinguished only if the department had filed its claim before the CoC and the claim was then admitted
options.B: survives, because an approved plan extinguishes only those claims that the plan has expressly rejected in writing
options.C: stands extinguished, since claims not forming part of the approved plan do not survive its approval
options.D: survives, because a plan binds only the financial creditors who voted on it and not the State as a claimant

questions.explanation: Ghanashyam Mishra holds that once a plan is approved, all claims not part of it stand extinguished.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A limits the binding effect to voting creditors. Option B reverses the rule by requiring an express rejection. Option D adds a requirement of earlier filing that the holding does not contain.
questions.clat_trap: Option three seems fair because it rewards diligence, yet the passage speaks of 'all claims'.
questions.language_trick: 'all claims not forming part of the plan' is wide and excludes any exception for claimants who stayed silent.

questions.question: A High Court holds that, under Essar Steel, an operational creditor must receive exactly the same percentage recovery as a financial creditor. The reasoning is

options.A: flawed, because under Essar an operational creditor has no entitlement to any payment under a resolution plan
options.B: sound, because the commercial wisdom of the CoC is justiciable whenever the distribution between creditors is challenged
options.C: sound, because equitable treatment in an insolvency means that every class of creditor must receive an identical share
options.D: flawed, because Essar speaks of equitable treatment and leaves the distribution within the commercial wisdom of the CoC

questions.explanation: Essar draws a line between equitable and equal treatment and holds the CoC's commercial wisdom non-justiciable.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads 'equitable' as 'equal', erasing the distinction drawn by the Court. Option B overstates and claims no entitlement. Option C contradicts the non-justiciability holding.
questions.clat_trap: The word pair 'equitable, not equal' is the whole question. Students who read 'equitable' as 'fair and therefore equal' fall into option one.
questions.language_trick: 'equitable, not equal' is deliberately contrasted in the passage.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct on the passage?
I. The Viswanathan Committee's report was a recommendation, and the Code is the enactment the courts test.
II. Essar Steel held the commercial wisdom of the CoC to be justiciable on fairness.
III. An approved resolution plan extinguishes all claims not forming part of it.
IV. The 2025 amendment Bill has been enacted and is in force.

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III are stated in the passage. Statement II reverses Essar. Statement IV is wrong because the Bill had only passed the Lok Sabha as of the passage and its status is to be verified.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option I, II and III includes II, which reverses Essar. Option II and IV includes both false statements. Option I, III and IV includes IV, which is unsupported.
questions.clat_trap: A statement that looks like a current-affairs fact (IV) is placed beside accurate case statements to tempt over-inclusion.
questions.language_trick: 'passed by the Lok Sabha' is not 'enacted'; a Bill needs both Houses and assent.

passages.title: The Irani Committee, the Companies Act 2013 and the Tribunal Cases
passages.passage: The Expert Committee on Company Law chaired by J J Irani (2005) recommended a modern, principle-based company statute. Its report led to the Companies Act, 2013, which provides for independent directors, at least one woman director on prescribed boards, corporate social responsibility under section 135, class actions by members and depositors under section 245, and the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and its Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) in place of the Company Law Board. The tribunal idea has an earlier history. The Eradi Committee (2000) led to the Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002. In Union of India v R Gandhi (2010), the Supreme Court held that Parliament may create the NCLT and NCLAT under Article 323B, inserted by the Forty-second Amendment, but that the provisions on qualifications and composition of the members offended judicial independence and the separation of powers, and directed amendments. A reconstituted NCLT and NCLAT were later upheld subject to safeguards on qualifications and independence. In L Chandra Kumar v Union of India (1997), the Court held that decisions of tribunals set up under Articles 323A and 323B remain subject to the High Court's scrutiny under Articles 226 and 227, since judicial review is part of the basic structure. In Tata Consultancy Services v Cyrus Investments (2021), the Court set aside the NCLAT order which had restored Cyrus Mistry as Executive Chairman of Tata Sons. It held that a case of oppression and mismanagement under section 241 requires conduct that is burdensome, harsh and wrongful, together with facts that would justify winding up on the just and equitable ground, and that the Articles of Association bind the company and its members in the manner of a contract.

questions.question: Which of the following is described in the passage as a feature of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: a right of members and depositors to bring a class action under section 245
options.B: retention of the Company Law Board as the principal body for hearing oppression complaints
options.C: an exemption from corporate social responsibility obligations for large companies
options.D: abolition of independent directors on the boards of listed companies

questions.explanation: The passage lists class actions by members and depositors under section 245 as a feature. It also records that the NCLT replaced the Company Law Board.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B contradicts the replacement of the Company Law Board by the NCLT. Option C contradicts the provision for independent directors. Option D contradicts section 135.
questions.clat_trap: Three options each contradict one feature listed in the first paragraph. Reading the list carefully removes them.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: After L Chandra Kumar, a party aggrieved by a decision of a tribunal constituted under Article 323B can

options.A: approach the High Court only if Parliament has expressly preserved that jurisdiction in the statute creating the tribunal in question
options.B: approach only the Supreme Court under Article 136, because Article 323B excludes the High Courts from the field of the tribunal altogether
options.C: invoke the High Court's jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 227, because judicial review is part of the basic structure
options.D: approach no court at all, because Article 323B was inserted to remove tribunal decisions from the reach of judicial review

questions.explanation: The Court held that tribunal decisions remain subject to High Court scrutiny. The power cannot be taken away by statute because it forms part of the basic structure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A accepts the ouster that the Court rejected. Option B extends the ouster to all courts. Option D makes High Court review depend on a statutory saving, which the basic structure holding makes unnecessary.
questions.clat_trap: Option three sounds like ordinary statutory construction, so it tempts students who forget that the source of review here is constitutional.
questions.language_trick: 'remain subject to' means the jurisdiction was never lost.

questions.question: A shareholder alleges oppression under section 241 only because the board removed the Executive Chairman in a manner the shareholder considers harsh. On Tata v Cyrus Investments, the allegation

options.A: is insufficient, because oppression can be shown only through a final winding up order made earlier by the competent tribunal on the same facts
options.B: is sufficient, provided the shareholder holds a stake large enough to qualify for the filing of an application under the Act, whatever the facts
options.C: is insufficient, since oppression needs conduct that is burdensome, harsh and wrongful and could justify just and equitable winding up
options.D: is sufficient, since any removal of a chairman without the chairman's consent amounts to oppression of all the shareholders who support him

questions.explanation: The test has two limbs. Conduct must be burdensome, harsh and wrongful, and the facts must be such that winding up would be just and equitable. Harshness alone does not make out oppression.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats removal alone as oppression. Option B turns a standing rule into a test of merit. Option D makes an earlier winding up order a precondition, which is not in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The word 'harsh' appears in the test, so an option that stresses harshness feels right. The second limb is what a student must remember.
questions.language_trick: 'together with' joins the two limbs; satisfying one is not enough.

questions.question: The Articles of Association of a company give a particular shareholder a right of consent over appointments to the board. A director is appointed without that consent. On the passage, the appointment

options.A: can be challenged as contrary to the Articles, which bind the company and its members in the manner of a contract
options.B: cannot be challenged, because the Articles are only internal guidelines and have no binding effect on company decisions
options.C: can be challenged only by the Registrar of Companies, since members have no standing to enforce the Articles
options.D: cannot be challenged, because the right of consent is valid only if it is also written into the Companies Act, 2013

questions.explanation: The Court treated the Articles as binding on the company and its members like a contract, so a breach is open to challenge.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B denies binding effect. Option C requires a statutory mirror for every clause. Option D denies the members any standing.
questions.clat_trap: A student who thinks that the Companies Act always overrides internal rules may choose the second option. The passage treats the Articles as contractual.
questions.language_trick: 'in the manner of a contract' sets the level of enforceability.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Parliament's power under Article 323B to create the NCLT did not by itself make the 2002 scheme valid. Reason (R): In R Gandhi, the Court held that the provisions on qualifications and composition of members had to respect judicial independence and the separation of powers.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Court accepted Parliament's competence but found the composition provisions defective. The reason given by the Court is the explanation for the assertion.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option two would apply if R were true but unrelated to A. Options three and four require one statement to be false, but both are accurate.
questions.clat_trap: Students may think that upholding Parliament's power means upholding the scheme. The passage separates competence from compliance.
questions.language_trick: 'did not by itself' signals that something more was required.

questions.question: Which of the following inferences is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: High Court review of tribunal decisions under Articles 226 and 227 survives the creation of tribunals under Article 323B
options.B: Since the NCLAT order was set aside in Tata v Cyrus, the Court held that Articles of Association can never bind a company like a contract
options.C: The Irani Committee's report was a recommendation which the legislature turned into the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: Parliament's power to create tribunals under Article 323B was accepted, though the 2002 provisions on members were found defective

questions.explanation: The passage says the Articles bind the company and its members in the manner of a contract, so the stated inference is the reverse of the holding.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D each restate something the passage says.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem makes the false statement the right answer. The false statement uses the case outcome (an order set aside) to suggest a contrary rule on Articles.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT supported' and the absolute 'can never' both signal the answer.

passages.title: Tax Committees, Vodafone and the End of Retrospective Taxation
passages.passage: Tax reform in India has often begun with expert committees. The Kelkar Task Force (2002) recommended rationalising indirect taxes, a step towards value added tax. The Parthasarathi Shome Committee (2012) examined the general anti-avoidance rule and the retrospective amendments relating to indirect transfers. The Easwar Committee (2016) suggested simplification of income-tax law and the Akhilesh Ranjan Committee (2017) worked on a new direct tax law. Such reports are persuasive; only legislation binds. In Union of India v Azadi Bachao Andolan (2003), the Supreme Court upheld CBDT Circular 789 and held that treaty shopping through Mauritius was not illegal. In Vodafone International Holdings v Union of India (2012), a three-judge Bench held that the indirect transfer of shares of a foreign company, which held Indian assets, was not taxable under section 9 of the Income Tax Act as it then stood. Parliament responded through the Finance Act, 2012, which inserted an Explanation operating retrospectively from 1962. In 2020, arbitral tribunals at The Hague, in the Vodafone and Cairn disputes, held that retrospective taxation breached the fair and equitable treatment standard under investment treaties. The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 then removed the retrospective demands and provided for refund of amounts collected, without interest. Article 265 provides that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law, and Article 246A, inserted by the One Hundred and First Amendment, gives Parliament and State legislatures simultaneous power over goods and services tax.

questions.question: Which pairing of committee and subject is consistent with the passage?

options.A: the Parthasarathi Shome Committee, with the introduction of Circular 789 on treaty shopping through Mauritius
options.B: the Easwar Committee, with the amendment inserting the retrospective Explanation in the Finance Act, 2012
options.C: the Akhilesh Ranjan Committee, with a task force on indirect taxes completed in 2002
options.D: the Kelkar Task Force, with the rationalisation of indirect taxes leading towards value added tax

questions.explanation: The Kelkar Task Force of 2002 dealt with indirect taxes. The other pairings mix committee names with unrelated subjects.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A attributes a CBDT circular to a 2012 committee. Option B credits the retrospective amendment to a committee that recommended simplification. Option C misdates the Akhilesh Ranjan Committee.
questions.clat_trap: All four committees are named in one sentence, so a careless match of name to subject is easy.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Under the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, amounts already collected under the retrospective demands were to be

options.A: refunded together with interest from the date of collection
options.B: retained by the exchequer, though no fresh demand could be raised
options.C: adjusted against future tax liabilities of the same assessees only
options.D: refunded to the assessees without any interest being paid on the amounts that had been collected

questions.explanation: The 2021 Act removed the retrospective demands and provided for refund without interest.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds interest, which the passage excludes. Option B keeps the money. Option C restricts the remedy to adjustment.
questions.clat_trap: The two words 'without interest' decide the question. Students expecting a full restitution select the interest option.
questions.language_trick: 'without interest' is a short qualifier that changes the remedy.

questions.question: A foreign company transferred shares of an overseas company that owned Indian assets in 2007. Applying the Vodafone judgment alone, before the Finance Act, 2012, the Indian tax authority

options.A: could tax it by lifting the corporate veil, because the commercial substance of the transaction lay in India
options.B: could not tax the transfer under section 9 as it then stood, since it was an indirect transfer outside the reach of the provision
options.C: could tax it only if the transferee were an Indian resident, whatever the wording of section 9
options.D: could tax it, because Article 265 permits tax on any transaction that has an economic effect on Indian assets

questions.explanation: The Court held that such an indirect transfer was not taxable under section 9 as then worded. Parliament later changed the law retrospectively.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reaches for veil-lifting, which the Court did not apply. Option C misuses Article 265, which requires authority of law. Option D adds a residence test that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The temporal trap is the phrase 'before the Finance Act, 2012'. After the Explanation the answer would be different.
questions.language_trick: 'as it then stood' ties the answer to the pre-amendment wording.

questions.question: A company claims the benefit of the India-Mauritius treaty and relies on Circular 789. On Azadi Bachao Andolan, the claim

options.A: must be rejected unless the company shows substantial economic activity carried on in Mauritius itself
options.B: cannot be rejected merely because it involves treaty shopping, which the Court held not to be illegal
options.C: succeeds only for the period before 2012, when the Explanation made all such claims taxable retrospectively
options.D: must be rejected, because the Court held treaty shopping to be an abuse of the treaty that warrants disallowing the benefit

questions.explanation: The Court upheld the Circular and held that treaty shopping through Mauritius was not illegal.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the opposite of the holding. Option C adds a substance test not found in the passage. Option D confuses a transfer-of-shares amendment with a treaty benefit.
questions.clat_trap: Because the later Vodafone events were hostile to the tax authority's position in some respects and favourable in others, students blend the two cases.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The 2020 arbitral findings against India did not by themselves repeal the retrospective Explanation. Reason (R): An arbitral finding under an investment treaty does not alter a domestic statute, and Parliament acted through the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Explanation was removed by Parliament in 2021. The tribunals found a treaty breach, but they could not amend domestic law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option two fits if R were true but did not explain A. Options three and four need a false statement, but both are accurate.
questions.clat_trap: Students tend to credit the arbitral findings with the repeal because the events are close in time. The passage shows that legislation, not arbitration, ended the retrospective regime.
questions.language_trick: 'by themselves' narrows the assertion to the direct effect of the findings.

questions.question: Which sequence of events is correct on the passage?

options.A: Hague arbitral findings, then the Vodafone judgment, then the Finance Act, 2012, then the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021
options.B: Vodafone judgment, then the Hague arbitral findings, then the Finance Act, 2012, then the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021
options.C: Finance Act, 2012, then the Vodafone judgment, then the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021, then the Hague arbitral findings
options.D: Vodafone judgment, then the Finance Act, 2012, then the Hague arbitral findings of 2020, then the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court decided Vodafone in January 2012. Parliament then inserted the retrospective Explanation in 2012. The tribunals ruled in 2020 and Parliament repealed the retrospective demands in 2021.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A puts the Finance Act before the judgment it responded to. Option B puts the arbitral findings before the events that caused them. Option C places the findings before the Finance Act.
questions.clat_trap: Sequence questions look easy but the three wrong options differ by a single swap. Anchoring on 'Parliament responded' fixes the first two events.
questions.language_trick: 'responded' and 'then removed' fix the order.

passages.title: The Second National Commission on Labour, the Labour Codes and Landmark Judgments
passages.passage: The Second National Commission on Labour (2002) recommended that the large body of central labour laws be rationalised into broad codes. Parliament enacted four Labour Codes between 2019 and 2020: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. The Government notified all four to come into force on 21 November 2025; the position on subordinate rules should be verified. A commission's recommendation does not bind; it was the codes that changed the law. Judicial decisions shaped the field before and alongside the codes. In Bangalore Water Supply v A Rajappa (1978), a seven-judge Bench defined 'industry' through a triple test: systematic activity, organised by cooperation between employer and employee, for the production or distribution of goods or services to satisfy human wants. Profit motive was held unnecessary. In Randhir Singh v Union of India (1982), the Court derived equal pay for equal work from Articles 14 and 16, read with Article 39(d). In State of Punjab v Jagjit Singh (2016), it held that temporary employees performing the same duties as regular employees are entitled at least to the minimum of the regular pay scale. In T K Rangarajan v Government of Tamil Nadu (2003), the Court held that there is no fundamental right to strike, and Article 19(1)(c) does not include one. Article 43 directs the State to secure a living wage, and Article 43A, inserted by the Forty-second Amendment, directs steps to secure workers' participation in management. Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 makes retrenchment conditional on one month's notice or wages in lieu, and on payment of compensation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of the test in Bangalore Water Supply for 'industry'?

options.A: a profit motive on the part of the employer, which the test does not make a condition of an enterprise being an industry
options.B: production or distribution of goods or services to satisfy human wants
options.C: an organised relationship between those who supply labour and those who direct it
options.D: systematic activity carried on with the cooperation of employer and employee

questions.explanation: The Court held that profit motive is unnecessary. The test turns on systematic activity, cooperation and the production or distribution of goods and services.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D state elements of the triple test or its organisation requirement.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem hides the answer among accurate statements. The one inaccurate item is the profit motive, which many students assume is essential to 'industry'.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT an element' flips the usual task.

questions.question: The principle of equal pay for equal work, as described in Randhir Singh, rests on

options.A: Article 43A on participation of workers in management read with Article 21
options.B: Articles 14 and 16, read with Article 39(d)
options.C: Article 43 on a living wage together with Article 19(1)(g)
options.D: Article 19(1)(c) on forming associations, read with Article 14

questions.explanation: The Court derived the principle from Articles 14 and 16, read with the directive in Article 39(d).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A uses a living wage directive and a trade freedom. Option C uses the participation directive. Option D uses the right to form associations.
questions.clat_trap: Directive principles are listed beside Part III rights in the passage, so options mix them. The directive of relevance to equal pay is Article 39(d), not Article 43.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question: A daily-wage worker performs the same duties as a regular employee on the same scale of responsibility. On Jagjit Singh, the worker is

options.A: entitled to every benefit of a regular employee, including pension, because the principle covers the whole service package
options.B: entitled to be regularised in service, because performance of identical duties creates a vested right to permanence
options.C: entitled at least to the minimum of the regular pay scale for the post, though not automatically to every service benefit
options.D: not entitled to the regular pay scale, since a temporary appointment excludes the claim of equal pay for equal work

questions.explanation: The Court limited the entitlement to the minimum of the regular pay scale. It did not grant regularisation or all benefits.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A denies the principle for temporary employees. Option B stretches it to permanence. Option D stretches it to all benefits.
questions.clat_trap: Both extremes are tempting. Option one is a plain reading of the rule that temporary employees get less, and options two and three overstate the relief.
questions.language_trick: 'at least' and 'minimum' set a floor, not a ceiling.

questions.question: A State dismisses employees who go on a prolonged, concerted strike. The employees challenge the dismissal only as a violation of Article 19(1)(c). On the passage, the challenge

options.A: is likely to succeed, since a living wage under Article 43 can be claimed only by employees who may withdraw their labour
options.B: is likely to succeed, since the right to form associations necessarily carries with it the right to strike as its lawful expression
options.C: is likely to fail, but only because the employees were in government service and not in an industrial establishment
options.D: is likely to fail on that ground, since there is no fundamental right to strike and Article 19(1)(c) does not include one

questions.explanation: Rangarajan holds that there is no fundamental right to strike, and Article 19(1)(c) does not include it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A converts a freedom to associate into a right to strike. Option B links a directive principle to a strike right. Option C adds a distinction between government and industrial employees that the holding does not turn on.
questions.clat_trap: Students who know that the right to form unions is fundamental may stretch it to strikes. The Court separated the two.
questions.language_trick: No specific language trick in this question.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct on the passage?
I. The Second National Commission on Labour recommended rationalising central labour laws into broad codes.
II. The four Labour Codes were notified to come into force on 21 November 2025.
III. Article 43A, inserted by the Forty-second Amendment, relates to workers' participation in management.
IV. Article 43 guarantees workers a fundamental right to strike.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, II and III restate the passage. Statement IV is false, since Article 43 is a directive on a living wage and the Court held there is no fundamental right to strike.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option I and II only omits III, which is accurate. Option II and IV includes the false IV. Option I, III and IV includes IV.
questions.clat_trap: Four statements and options with different combinations invite a student to include a statement that sounds plausible. Statement IV mixes a directive principle with a right the Court denied.
questions.language_trick: 'guarantees' and 'fundamental right' are the false features of statement IV.

questions.question: A worker is retrenched with wages in lieu of one month's notice but receives no retrenchment compensation. On section 25F as described, the retrenchment is

options.A: compliant, because payment of wages in lieu of notice is a complete substitute for every other condition of retrenchment
options.B: non-compliant only if the worker also fails to receive a written notice stating the reasons for the retrenchment
options.C: compliant, because compensation is payable only if the worker has completed a minimum number of years of service
options.D: non-compliant, since the section requires both notice, or wages in lieu, and the payment of compensation

questions.explanation: Retrenchment is conditional on notice (or wages in lieu) and on compensation. Wages in lieu satisfy only the first.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats one condition as enough. Option B adds a service threshold not found in the passage. Option C adds a written-reasons condition not found in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The words 'and on payment of compensation' are easy to overlook when the notice limb has been met.
questions.language_trick: 'and' joins two conditions that must both be met.

passages.title: The Ayyangar and Mashelkar Reports and the Judicial Treatment of Patents, Marks and Copyright
passages.passage: The Ayyangar Committee (1959) examined the patent law inherited from colonial times. Its report led to the Patents Act, 1970, which allowed patents on processes, and not products, in the fields of food and medicines. After the TRIPS Agreement (1995), the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2005 introduced product patents, and section 3(d) was kept to restrict patents on new forms of known substances unless enhanced therapeutic efficacy is shown. The Mashelkar Committee (2006), a technical expert group, advised against limiting product patents to new chemical entities; its advice is a recommendation and not law. In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court refused a patent for the beta crystalline form of imatinib mesylate, because no enhanced therapeutic efficacy over the known substance was shown under section 3(d). A Controller's order granting a compulsory licence for a cancer drug to an Indian manufacturer illustrates section 84, under which a licence can follow if the invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price. In Monsanto v Nuziveedu (2019), concerning a Bt cotton trait patent, the Supreme Court set aside a Delhi High Court Division Bench ruling that had held the patent invalid at an interlocutory stage and left the question of validity for trial; section 3(j) excludes plants and seeds from patentability, but the Court did not finally decide the status of such trait patents. In Cadila Health v Cadila Pharmaceuticals (2001), the Court held that for pharmaceutical products the test of deceptive similarity must be applied with greater caution, since confusion can harm health; relevant factors include the nature of the goods, the class of purchasers and the mode of purchase. Amritdhara Pharmacy v Satya Deo Gupta (1963) frames the test by reference to a purchaser of average intelligence and imperfect recollection. In Eastern Book Company v D B Modak (2008), the Court required a modicum of creativity for copyright in an edited law report.

questions.question: Following the Ayyangar Committee's report, the Patents Act, 1970 permitted, in the fields of food and medicines,

options.A: patents on processes of manufacture, but not on the products themselves
options.B: patents on both processes and products, if enhanced efficacy was shown
options.C: no patents of any kind, on the principle that such inventions belong to the public
options.D: patents on products, but not on processes of manufacture

questions.explanation: The 1970 Act allowed process patents for food and medicines. Product patents came only with the 2005 amendment after TRIPS.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the position. Option C imports the s.3(d) efficacy test, which concerns new forms of known substances. Option D denies any patent.
questions.clat_trap: The 1970 and 2005 regimes are described together, so a student can reverse them. The reversal option looks as plausible as the correct one.
questions.language_trick: 'processes, and not products' draws the line.

questions.question: A company seeks a patent for a new salt form of a known drug and shows only the same efficacy as the known substance. On Novartis, the application

options.A: succeeds, because a new salt form is a different substance and the 2005 amendment allows product patents on all new forms
options.B: is refused only because a compulsory licence under section 84 would otherwise be required for the drug
options.C: is liable to be refused under section 3(d), unless enhanced therapeutic efficacy over the known substance is shown
options.D: succeeds, because the Court in Novartis decided only the case of a crystalline form and did not touch other forms of drugs

questions.explanation: Section 3(d) restricts patents on new forms of known substances unless enhanced efficacy is shown. Novartis applied it.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A ignores section 3(d). Option B confines the case to crystalline forms, though the test applies to new forms of known substances. Option D confuses patentability with the grant of a compulsory licence.
questions.clat_trap: Options one and two appeal to the narrowness of the case. The passage states the rule in terms of 'new forms of known substances'.
questions.language_trick: 'unless' shows that section 3(d) is a condition, not an absolute bar.

questions.question: Which description of the Mashelkar Committee's advice is accurate on the passage?

options.A: It recommended product patents only for new chemical entities, and Parliament enacted that limit in section 3(d) of the Act
options.B: It introduced product patents in 2006 by a binding direction to the Controller, which later became section 84
options.C: It advised restoring the process-patent-only regime of 1970 for medicines, which Parliament accepted in 2005
options.D: It advised against restricting product patents to new chemical entities, but this was a recommendation and not law

questions.explanation: The committee advised against limiting product patents to new chemical entities. The report was a recommendation, and Parliament's own amendment of 2005 shaped the law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the advice and treats a recommendation as law. Option B makes a committee's report binding. Option C reverses the history, since the 2005 amendment introduced product patents.
questions.clat_trap: The date of the Mashelkar report (2006) is after the 2005 amendment, so an option that connects them causally is wrong.
questions.language_trick: 'advised against' is the key verb.

questions.question: Two pharmaceutical marks are similar in sound and are used for prescription medicines bought mainly through pharmacists. On Cadila Health, the Court will

options.A: apply the deceptive similarity test with added caution, weighing the nature of the goods, the class of purchasers and the mode of purchase
options.B: treat the marks as dissimilar if the medicines are prescribed by trained doctors, since confusion among informed purchasers is then impossible in practice
options.C: decide only on the visual similarity of the marks, since the class of purchasers is relevant only to non-medical goods
options.D: apply the ordinary test, since doctors and pharmacists are trained persons whose professional care removes any need for a stricter approach to similarity

questions.explanation: Cadila requires greater caution for pharmaceutical products, since confusion can harm health, and lists the factors relevant to the inquiry.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B and Option C ignore the added caution. Option D limits the factors to appearance and excludes the factors the passage lists.
questions.clat_trap: Students may think that the expertise of doctors dilutes the risk of confusion. The Court looked at the consequence of confusion, which is health harm.
questions.language_trick: 'greater caution' sets a higher standard of care for the decision-maker.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Copyright can subsist in an edited version of a court judgment. Reason (R): In Eastern Book Company v D B Modak, the Court required a modicum of creativity for copyright in an edited law report.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The test applied by the Court is the modicum of creativity. Where the editing meets that test, the edited version can attract copyright. The reason is the explanation for the assertion.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option two would fit if R were true but beside the point. Options three and four need a false statement, but both are accurate.
questions.clat_trap: Students may assume that no one can own anything connected with a public judgment. The passage separates the raw text from the creative edit.
questions.language_trick: 'a modicum of creativity' means a minimal creative contribution, not a high one.

questions.question: Which statement about Monsanto v Nuziveedu (2019) is accurate on the passage?

options.A: The Court held that trait patents on plants are invalid because section 3(j) excludes plants and seeds from patentability
options.B: The Court held that the Plant Variety and Farmers' Rights Act bars every patent connected with agricultural seeds
options.C: The Court upheld the patent in final form and directed the licensees to pay royalties on the Bt cotton trait
options.D: The Court set aside an interlocutory ruling that had invalidated the patent, and left the question of validity open for determination at trial

questions.explanation: The Court set aside the Division Bench's interlocutory invalidation and left validity to trial. It did not finally decide the status of trait patents.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads the exclusion in section 3(j) as the holding. Option B converts a procedural order into a final upholding. Option C invents a bar based on the 1970 Act's neighbour statute.
questions.clat_trap: The passage mentions section 3(j), which tempts students to treat it as the ratio. The Court's order was about the procedural stage.
questions.language_trick: 'at an interlocutory stage' and 'left the question for trial' mark the limit of the decision.

passages.title: Raghavan Committee, the Competition Act 2002 and the Judgments that Shaped the CCI
passages.passage: The Raghavan Committee on Competition Policy and Law (2000) concluded that the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969, which policed size and concentration, no longer suited an open economy, and it recommended a law aimed at conduct that harms competition. The Competition Act, 2002 followed. It prohibits anti-competitive agreements (section 3), abuse of dominant position (section 4) and combinations that cause or are likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition (sections 5 and 6), and it created the Competition Commission of India (CCI). In Brahm Dutt v Union of India (2005), the Supreme Court upheld the Act, but observed that the Commission's advisory and adjudicatory roles sat uneasily together and that adjudicatory functions should be separated from advisory ones; the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2007 then created an appellate tribunal, whose functions now lie with the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal after the Finance Act, 2017. In SAIL v Competition Commission of India (2010), the Court held that an order under section 26(1), forming a prima facie opinion and directing investigation, is administrative and does not call for a prior hearing of the party. In Competition Commission of India v Bharti Airtel (2018), the Court held that the Commission has jurisdiction over competition issues in the telecom sector, though the sectoral regulator should first determine technical questions within its own domain. In Excel Crop Care v Competition Commission of India (2017), the Court held that a penalty is to be computed on the relevant turnover and not on the total turnover of the enterprise. The Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced settlement and commitment procedures, a deal-value threshold for notifying combinations and leniency plus, and it provides for penalties by reference to global turnover. The Constitution places commercial and industrial monopolies in Entry 21 of the Concurrent List, while Article 39(b) and (c) of the directive principles speak against concentration of wealth.

questions.question: The central shift in approach that the Raghavan Committee recommended was from

options.A: regulating the size and concentration of enterprises to regulating conduct that harms competition
options.B: controlling the prices of essential goods to controlling the quantity of imported goods
options.C: prosecution of cartels as crimes to a purely civil adjudication of business disputes
options.D: state ownership of dominant enterprises to private ownership under licence conditions

questions.explanation: The passage says the MRTP Act policed size and concentration, while the Committee wanted a law aimed at conduct that harms competition.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B brings in price and import control, which the passage never mentions. Option C invents a privatisation recommendation. Option D describes a procedural change that the Committee is not said to have proposed.
questions.clat_trap: All three wrong options are 'shift from X to Y' sentences with an economic flavour, so a candidate who knows only that the Act is pro-market may be drawn to them.
questions.language_trick: 'from ... to ...' fixes both ends; the passage gives the 'from' end (size and concentration) explicitly.

questions.question: The CCI forms a prima facie opinion under section 26(1) and directs an investigation into an enterprise without hearing it first. The enterprise challenges the order for breach of natural justice. On the passage, the challenge is

options.A: likely to fail, because the section confers no right of challenge at any stage of the proceedings
options.B: likely to succeed, because every order of a quasi-judicial body requires prior notice and hearing
options.C: likely to fail, because such an order is administrative in nature, with no final determination of rights, and the hearing comes at the later stage
options.D: likely to succeed, because the Act obliges the Commission to hear an enterprise before any investigation order

questions.explanation: SAIL treats the section 26(1) order as administrative, so no prior hearing is needed. The party is heard when the inquiry proceeds.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A generalises natural justice to every step of a quasi-judicial body. Option B attributes a statutory hearing duty that the passage does not mention. Option D reaches the right outcome for a wrong reason, because the passage says nothing about the absence of any challenge.
questions.clat_trap: Option Option D gives the same outcome as the right option, so a hurried reader may choose it. The CLAT test is the reasoning, not just the result.
questions.language_trick: 'administrative' versus 'quasi-judicial' is the whole point of the case.

questions.question: An enterprise has a total turnover of 1,000 units, of which 100 units come from the relevant product in which the CCI finds an abuse of dominance. Under Excel Crop Care alone, the ceiling on the penalty would be computed on

options.A: the 1,000 units, because a penalty must follow the enterprise as a whole
options.B: neither figure, since the Act fixes the penalty as a stated sum of money
options.C: an average of the two turnover figures, to balance deterrence with proportionality
options.D: the 100 units from the relevant product alone and not on the 1,000 units of the enterprise's total turnover

questions.explanation: Excel Crop Care requires penalty to be computed on relevant turnover.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is the position that Excel Crop Care rejected. Option B invents a blended test. Option C denies that turnover plays any role.
questions.clat_trap: The 2023 amendment (global turnover) sits in the same passage and pulls the student to the total figure. The stem says 'under Excel Crop Care alone' to block that.
questions.language_trick: 'alone' confines the answer to one judgment and excludes the later amendment.

questions.question: A telecom operator is alleged to have abused its dominance through discriminatory interconnection terms. On the passage as read with Bharti Airtel, the correct position is that

options.A: the CCI may decide even the technical interconnection questions without any reference to the sectoral regulator, since competition law prevails over it
options.B: the CCI's jurisdiction is not ousted, though the sectoral regulator should first settle the technical questions in its field
options.C: the CCI acquires jurisdiction only after the sectoral regulator has imposed a penalty on the operator for the same conduct
options.D: only the sectoral regulator may act, because the telecom statute is a complete code that wholly excludes the operation of the Competition Act

questions.explanation: The Court held the Commission has jurisdiction but the regulator should first determine technical questions within its domain.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads the telecom law as a complete code, which the Court rejected. Option C ignores the role of the sectoral regulator. Option D makes the CCI's jurisdiction depend on a penalty, which the passage does not support.
questions.clat_trap: Both extremes (ousting and ignoring the regulator) are offered, and the middle position is the correct one.
questions.language_trick: 'though' and 'first' mark the two-step position.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: The Commission's jurisdiction in telecom was affirmed, with a role reserved for the sectoral regulator on technical questions of the sector
options.B: Entry 21 of the Concurrent List concerns commercial and industrial monopolies, which supports Parliament's competence in this field
options.C: The 2007 amendment responded to the concern over combined advisory and adjudicatory roles within the Commission, as the passage explains
options.D: Brahm Dutt held the Competition Act unconstitutional until adjudicatory functions were moved

questions.explanation: Brahm Dutt upheld the Act while observing that the functions should be separated. It did not strike the Act down.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option B and Option C are each supported by the passage.
questions.clat_trap: A negative stem ('NOT') with a first-look plausible 'unconstitutional until' story. Court observations are confused with a declaration of invalidity.
questions.language_trick: 'upheld' versus 'held unconstitutional'; 'observed' versus 'held'.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Competition Act, 2002 follows the Raghavan Committee's recommendation to retain the MRTP Act's control over the size of enterprises. Reason (R): The Act prohibits abuse of dominant position under section 4.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The Committee recommended moving away from size-based control towards conduct-based control, so A is false. R states section 4 correctly.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A is false because the Committee found the size-based approach unsuited to an open economy.
questions.clat_trap: R is a true statement placed beside a false one. A candidate may match two Competition Act phrases and choose a 'both true' option.
questions.language_trick: 'retain' reverses the Committee's recommendation.

passages.title: From Law Commission to Srikrishna Committee: Reforming Arbitration in India
passages.passage: The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 was modelled on the UNCITRAL Model Law of 1985. The 246th Report of the Law Commission (2014) led to the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2015. It added the Fifth and Seventh Schedules listing grounds that give rise to doubts as to an arbitrator's independence or impartiality, introduced section 12(5), narrowed the 'public policy' ground for setting aside awards under section 34 and added 'patent illegality' as a ground for domestic awards, ended the automatic stay of an award on filing a challenge (section 36), and set a time limit for completing domestic arbitrations (section 29A). The Srikrishna Committee (2017) on institutionalisation of arbitration led to the 2019 amendment, which provided for an Arbitration Council of India, though that body has yet to be operationalised (verify current status). In BALCO v Kaiser Aluminium (2012), a five-judge Bench held that Part I of the Act does not apply to arbitrations seated outside India, and applied the holding prospectively from 6 September 2012. In BCCI v Kochi Cricket (2018), the Court held that the 2015 amendment to section 36 applies to court proceedings commenced after 23 October 2015, whether or not the arbitration began earlier. In Ssangyong Engineering v NHAI (2019), the Court held that patent illegality does not allow a court to re-appreciate evidence. In TRF Ltd v Energo Engineering (2017) and Perkins Eastman v HSCC (2019), the Court held that a person who is ineligible to act as arbitrator cannot nominate one, and that unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator by one party is invalid. In Cox and Kings v SAP India (2023), a Constitution Bench recognised the group of companies doctrine, and in the Interplay reference (2023, seven judges) it was held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is not void but is inadmissible until stamped.

questions.question: A party to a foreign-seated arbitration under an agreement made before 6 September 2012 seeks Part I interim relief from an Indian court in 2010. On BALCO as described, the position is that

options.A: Part I is available only if the parties have agreed to Indian procedural rules for the arbitration
options.B: Part I is unavailable, because BALCO applies its holding to every agreement made earlier
options.C: the earlier law governs the case, because the new rule operates only prospectively from 6 September 2012
options.D: Part I is available, because BALCO concerned only final awards and not interim relief

questions.explanation: BALCO was applied only from 6 September 2012. For earlier agreements, the previous position continued.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses prospectivity. Option B adds a distinction between awards and interim relief that the passage does not draw. Option D imports a condition from the wrong source.
questions.clat_trap: A holding about the territorial reach of Part I (foreign seat) is mixed with the question of the date from which it operates.
questions.language_trick: 'prospectively' decides the case; the question asks about an event in 2010.

questions.question: A contract provides that the managing director of one party may appoint a sole arbitrator. The other party challenges the appointment. On the passage, the challenge is likely to

options.A: fail, because ineligibility affects an arbitrator but not the person who nominates one
options.B: succeed only if the managing director personally signed the contract on behalf of the party
options.C: succeed, because the unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator by one party is invalid
options.D: fail, because the parties agreed to the clause and party autonomy is absolute in appointments

questions.explanation: Perkins Eastman held that unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator is invalid, and TRF held that an ineligible person cannot nominate.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats party autonomy as absolute. Option B invents a condition about who signed. Option D contradicts TRF, which the passage reports.
questions.clat_trap: Party autonomy sounds like the foundation of arbitration, which makes the absolute statement feel respectable.
questions.language_trick: 'absolute' is the overstated word.

questions.question: A court is asked to set aside a domestic award on the ground that the tribunal wrongly weighed the evidence on a disputed fact. On the passage, the court

options.A: may do so if it records reasons why the tribunal's view of the evidence is plainly unreasonable
options.B: must do so, since a wrong finding of fact is itself a patent illegality that the court is bound to correct
options.C: may do so if the error is apparent on a fresh reading of the record by the court
options.D: cannot, since patent illegality does not permit re-appreciation of evidence

questions.explanation: Ssangyong holds that patent illegality does not permit a court to re-appreciate evidence.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A equates any factual error with patent illegality. Option B and Option C permit re-appreciation by an alternative route.
questions.clat_trap: Three options look like a diligent court reviewing an unfair award. The correct option requires restraint.
questions.language_trick: 're-appreciate' is a term of art for a second look at evidence.

questions.question: A claimant files a petition for the appointment of an arbitrator, relying on an agreement that has not been stamped. On the Interplay reference as described, the correct approach is that

options.A: the agreement is admissible and stamp duty is waived altogether because arbitration is treated as a special statutory regime of its own
options.B: the court may not reject the petition as based on a void agreement, though the agreement stays inadmissible until the defect is cured
options.C: the tribunal may never proceed, even after duty and penalty are paid on the agreement, as the defect is incurable
options.D: the petition must be dismissed at the threshold, since an unstamped agreement is void and non-existent in the eye of the law

questions.explanation: The seven-judge reference held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is not void but inadmissible until stamped, which is a curable defect.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats the defect as fatal. Option C waives the duty altogether. Option D treats the defect as incurable even after payment.
questions.clat_trap: Older authority treated unstamped agreements as non-existent, and a student relying on it chooses the first wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'void' versus 'inadmissible until stamped' changes the whole result.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct on the passage?
I. The 2015 amendment to section 36 applies to court proceedings commenced after 23 October 2015, whether or not the arbitration began earlier.
II. Patent illegality allows courts to re-appreciate the evidence before the tribunal.
III. BALCO applied its holding on Part I prospectively.
IV. The Arbitration Council of India under the 2019 amendment is fully operational and administers all institutional arbitration.

options.A: II and III only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I and III restate the passage. Statement II contradicts Ssangyong. Statement IV is contradicted by the passage, which says the Council has yet to be operationalised.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II reverses Ssangyong. IV claims a body is functioning when the passage says it is not.
questions.clat_trap: Combinations that pair one true statement with a false one are common in four-option statement questions.
questions.language_trick: 'whether or not' in I is a statement about the stage at which the arbitration began.

questions.question: The change in arbitration law that is traceable to the Srikrishna Committee, as distinct from the Law Commission's 246th Report, is

options.A: provision for an Arbitration Council of India under the 2019 amendment
options.B: the narrowing of public policy and addition of patent illegality in section 34
options.C: the addition of the Fifth and Seventh Schedules on arbitrator independence
options.D: the ending of the automatic stay of an award on challenge under section 36

questions.explanation: The passage ties the 2019 amendment and the Council to the Srikrishna Committee. The other changes came from the 2015 Act.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are all features of the 2015 amendment that followed the Law Commission's report.
questions.clat_trap: Both reforms are discussed together, so a student has to attribute each change to the right body.
questions.language_trick: 'as distinct from' signals a matching task.

passages.title: International Bodies, Treaty Obligations and Indian Courts
passages.passage: The International Law Commission, established by the General Assembly in 1947 to promote the codification and progressive development of international law, produced the Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts in 2001. Under them, a State commits an internationally wrongful act when conduct attributable to it breaches an international obligation, and the circumstances that preclude wrongfulness include consent, self-defence and countermeasures. UN treaty bodies such as the Human Rights Committee under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the CEDAW Committee review State reports. The Human Rights Committee may receive individual communications only against States that have accepted the First Optional Protocol, which India has not done. Their views are authoritative but are not binding judgments. India ratified the ICCPR in 1979 with reservations and declarations. Article 51(c) of the Constitution directs the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, Article 253 empowers Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties, and treaty-making is an executive function. In Gramophone Co. v Birendra Bahadur Pandey (1984), the Supreme Court held that rules of international law that do not conflict with municipal law are part of Indian law, but that where there is conflict, municipal law prevails. In Vishaka (1997), the Court relied on CEDAW to frame guidelines on sexual harassment where domestic law was silent, reading international conventions into the meaning of fundamental rights where they are consistent with them. In Jolly Varghese v Bank of Cochin (1980), the Court read Article 11 of the ICCPR with Article 21 in finding that imprisonment merely for inability to fulfil a contractual obligation is impermissible. In the Jadhav case (India v Pakistan, 2019), the International Court of Justice held by a large majority that Pakistan had violated Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations by failing to inform Mr Jadhav of his rights and denying consular access, and ordered effective review and reconsideration of his conviction and sentence, but declined to order his release.

questions.question: A citizen of India wishes to file an individual communication with the UN Human Rights Committee alleging a violation of ICCPR rights by India. On the passage,

options.A: this is open only after the Supreme Court has rejected a petition on the same facts
options.B: this is open to the citizen, because India ratified the ICCPR in 1979 and ratification itself confers individual access
options.C: this is not open to the citizen, because India has not accepted the First Optional Protocol
options.D: this is open to the citizen, and the Committee's view would operate as a binding judgment on India

questions.explanation: Individual communications lie only against States that have accepted the First Optional Protocol, and India has not.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats ratification of the Covenant as enough. Option B invents an exhaustion rule as a condition for access. Option D wrongly makes the Committee's views binding.
questions.clat_trap: Ratification and acceptance of the individual complaint procedure are different acts, and the options trade on that confusion.
questions.language_trick: 'only against States that have accepted' is a restrictive phrase.

questions.question: A statute enacted by Parliament conflicts with a customary rule of international law. On Gramophone as described, an Indian court will

options.A: apply the customary rule, but only if it is also found in a treaty ratified by India
options.B: apply the customary rule, since Article 51(c) places it above statutes of Parliament
options.C: apply the statute, since municipal law prevails over conflicting international law
options.D: strike down the statute under Article 13 for contravening international law

questions.explanation: Gramophone says that where there is conflict, municipal law prevails.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A converts a directive principle into a supremacy clause. Option B applies Article 13 to a source it does not cover. Option D invents a ratification condition for a rule that would not apply in any case.
questions.clat_trap: Article 51(c) sounds mandatory, but it is a directive principle and does not displace a statute.
questions.language_trick: 'conflicting' is the hinge; the passage allows international rules only where there is no conflict.

questions.question: In Vishaka, reliance on CEDAW was permissible in the absence of domestic law because

options.A: the Court held that CEDAW is a binding treaty enforceable by a writ in its own terms
options.B: Parliament had already used Article 253 to implement CEDAW through a special statute
options.C: treaties ratified by India become part of domestic law automatically, without any legislation
options.D: international conventions consistent with fundamental rights can be read into them to fill a legislative gap

questions.explanation: The Court read consistent conventions into the meaning of fundamental rights where domestic law was silent.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a monist rule that India does not follow. Option B claims direct enforceability. Option C says Parliament had legislated, but the passage says domestic law was silent.
questions.clat_trap: Dualism versus incorporation is the difference between the correct and the first wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'consistent with' and 'where silent' limit the rule.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an accurate statement on the passage?
