options.A: The ICJ held that Pakistan had breached Article 36 of the Vienna Convention
options.B: In Jadhav, the ICJ ordered Mr Jadhav's release because consular access had been denied
options.C: The ICJ ordered effective review and reconsideration of the conviction and sentence
options.D: Treaty body views are authoritative but are not binding judgments

questions.explanation: The ICJ declined to order release and ordered effective review and reconsideration instead.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D state the passage accurately.
questions.clat_trap: A negatively worded stem where the incorrect option is the dramatic, familiar outcome (release).
questions.language_trick: 'ordered ... release' is the unsupported verb.

questions.question: State X's armed forces breach a treaty obligation, and X says that it never gave the order and that its army acted on its own. Under the Articles on State Responsibility as described, the first issue is

options.A: whether the conduct is attributable to the State, since armed forces are an organ of the State
options.B: whether the obligation breached is also contained in the municipal law of X
options.C: whether the injured State had consented to the breach before it occurred
options.D: whether the Human Rights Committee has accepted individual communications against X under the First Optional Protocol

questions.explanation: An internationally wrongful act requires conduct attributable to the State and a breach of an international obligation. Armed forces are an organ of the State, so attribution is the first step.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns to a procedure that belongs to individual petitions. Option C jumps to a circumstance precluding wrongfulness, which is relevant only once attribution and breach are established. Option D makes the international wrong depend on domestic law.
questions.clat_trap: The question is about order of analysis, and three options discuss real concepts out of sequence.
questions.language_trick: 'first issue' asks for sequence, not for every relevant factor.

questions.question: Assertion (A): An Indian court can use CEDAW to fill a gap in domestic law even though India has not enacted a statute implementing it. Reason (R): Under Gramophone, rules of international law that conflict with municipal law prevail over it.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: Vishaka supports A, since consistent conventions can be read into fundamental rights where domestic law is silent. R is false, as Gramophone says municipal law prevails where there is conflict.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R reverses Gramophone, so any option that treats R as true fails.
questions.clat_trap: R is false but sits in a context where the real rule is its opposite, and the same case is mentioned in both.
questions.language_trick: 'prevail over it' reverses the direction of supremacy.

passages.title: Forests, Expert Committees and the 42nd Amendment
passages.passage: In T. N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v Union of India (1996), the Supreme Court gave 'forest' its dictionary meaning irrespective of ownership or classification, extended the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 to areas that are forests in fact, and kept the case alive as a continuing mandamus. In 2002 it set up the Central Empowered Committee to monitor compliance and examine applications. The 42nd Amendment (1976) had inserted Article 48A, which directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife, and Article 51A(g), which makes protection of the environment a duty of citizens; it also moved forests and the protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A and 17B). Expert committees have shaped the law as well. The Gadgil Committee (2011) and the Kasturirangan Committee (2013) examined the Western Ghats and proposed ecologically sensitive areas with different degrees of restriction, and the T. S. R. Subramanian Committee (2014) was asked to review environmental laws. The Law Commission's 186th Report (2003) recommended specialised environmental courts, which led to the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v Union of India (1996), the Court held that the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of the environmental law of the country, and that the onus of proof lies on the actor or developer to show that the activity is environmentally benign. The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023, renamed the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, confines the Act to land notified as forest or recorded as forest in government records on or after 25 October 1980, and exempts categories such as linear projects along railways and roads, security-related infrastructure within 100 km of borders, and zoos and eco-tourism facilities. In February 2024 the Supreme Court directed that, until the States and Union Territories consolidate their records, the dictionary meaning of forest recognised in Godavarman should continue to apply (an interim position; verify current status).

questions.question: The effect of the 42nd Amendment on the constitutional treatment of forests was to

options.A: give Parliament exclusive power over forests by moving them to the Union List, removing the States' role in the subject altogether
options.B: repeal the State List entry on forests and leave the field to Article 51A, which then operates as a source of power
options.C: move forests and the protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List
options.D: convert the State's duty under Article 48A into a justiciable fundamental right enforceable by every citizen through writ petitions

questions.explanation: The passage says the 42nd Amendment moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List, and inserted Articles 48A and 51A(g).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses concurrent with exclusive power. Option B turns a directive principle into a fundamental right. Option D misdescribes Article 51A(g) as a source of legislative power.
questions.clat_trap: Concurrent, Union and State List language is used in the options to make small differences look like large ones.
questions.language_trick: 'exclusive' versus 'concurrent'.

questions.question: A patch of land has tree cover but is not notified as forest and is not recorded as forest in any government record. Reading the 2023 Act alone and the interim position of February 2024 together, the better view is that

options.A: the Central Empowered Committee must first classify it as forest or non-forest before either regime can apply to the land
options.B: the 2023 Act would not cover it, though the interim direction keeps the dictionary meaning alive for now
options.C: the 2023 Act covers it, because forest in the Act means any land that has tree cover, whether recorded or not
options.D: it is wholly outside protection, because the 2024 direction revived only recorded forests and nothing else

questions.explanation: The 2023 Act is confined to notified or recorded forest. The 2024 interim direction continues the Godavarman meaning until records are consolidated.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the position that the 2023 Act replaced. Option C gets the interim direction backwards. Option D invents a gatekeeping role for the Committee.
questions.clat_trap: The stem asks for the result of two instruments read together, and a student who stops at the Act chooses the wrong option.
questions.language_trick: 'alone' and 'together' mark the two layers of analysis.

questions.question: A factory's process may seriously harm a river, but the scientific evidence is incomplete. On the principles in Vellore as described, the burden of showing that the process is safe

options.A: lies on the industry proposing the activity, since uncertainty does not justify delay in preventing harm
options.B: lies on no one, until the Central Empowered Committee has examined the process
options.C: lies on the State, which must show that the process is unsafe before any restraint
options.D: lies on the residents who allege harm, since they must prove damage before relief

questions.explanation: Vellore places the onus of proof on the actor or developer under the precautionary principle.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B places the burden on the victim, which is the position the precautionary principle reverses. Option C puts it on the State. Option D invents a committee prerequisite.
questions.clat_trap: In ordinary litigation the burden lies on the person who alleges, so a student defaults to that rule.
questions.language_trick: 'onus of proof' is the key phrase.

questions.question: A recommendation of the Kasturirangan Committee about the Western Ghats is best understood as

options.A: binding on all States from the date of submission, as the Committee was set up by the Supreme Court
options.B: advisory in nature, effective only if accepted through executive notification or legislation
options.C: an order of the Central Empowered Committee carrying contempt consequences
options.D: a direction under Article 48A that Parliament must enforce

questions.explanation: The Gadgil and Kasturirangan Committees were expert committees whose reports have to be accepted by the government. The Central Empowered Committee was the Court's body.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A confuses an expert committee with a court-appointed one. Option C misreads Article 48A. Option D confuses it with the monitoring body.
questions.clat_trap: The options mix two committees that appear in the same passage, only one of which was set up by the Court.
questions.language_trick: 'advisory' versus 'binding'.

questions.question: Which change introduced by the 2023 Act narrows protection compared with the position in Godavarman?

options.A: Extending the Act to plantations with tree cover on any private land
options.B: Adopting the precautionary principle as a binding rule inside the Act
options.C: Limiting the Act to land notified or recorded as forest, instead of the dictionary meaning of forest
options.D: Requiring Central approval for every use of forest land within 100 km of borders

questions.explanation: Godavarman used the dictionary meaning irrespective of classification. The 2023 Act confines the law to notified or recorded forest.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the opposite of what the Act does. Option B reverses the border exemption. Option D is not stated in the passage.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option sounds protective, and the question asks for the narrowing change, so a student must resist the pro-environment instinct.
questions.language_trick: 'narrows' asks for a reduction in coverage.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct on the passage?
I. The Central Empowered Committee was set up by the Supreme Court in 2002.
II. The Law Commission's 186th Report led to the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
III. The 2023 Act exempts security-related infrastructure within 100 km of borders.
IV. Godavarman limited the 1980 Act to notified forests only.

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I, II and III only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, III and IV only

questions.explanation: Statements I, II and III restate the passage. Statement IV is wrong because Godavarman used the dictionary meaning irrespective of classification.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A candidate who misses III chooses the first option. IV reverses Godavarman.
questions.clat_trap: Three true statements with one false are easy to mark in a hurry, and omitting one true statement is the common error.
questions.language_trick: 'only' in IV is the false limitation.

passages.title: Unfair Terms in Contracts: The 199th Law Commission Report and Judicial Responses
passages.passage: The Law Commission of India's 199th Report (2006) on unfair procedural and substantive terms in contracts recommended legislation to deal with such terms, since the Indian Contract Act, 1872 has no general doctrine of unfair terms (verify current status). Courts have filled part of the gap with section 23, which treats as void an agreement whose object or consideration is opposed to public policy, and with Article 14 where a State instrumentality is a party. In Central Inland Water Transport Corporation v Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986), the Court struck down a rule that allowed termination of permanent employees of a government company on notice without reasons, holding it unconscionable and violative of section 23 and Article 14 because of the gross inequality of bargaining power. In Life Insurance Corporation v Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995), the Court examined standard-form terms in insurance policies and held that State instrumentalities must act fairly in standard-form contracts. Courts distinguish unconscionability from undue influence under section 16, which requires that one party be in a position to dominate the will of the other and use that position to obtain an unfair advantage. Section 74 provides that where a sum is named as payable on breach, the party complaining is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named. In Fateh Chand v Balkrishan Dass (1963), the Court held that the named sum is only a ceiling and that the party complaining may recover reasonable compensation only. In Kailash Nath Associates v DDA (2015), the Court held that where loss can be proved a party must prove it, and that proof is dispensed with only where loss is difficult or impossible to assess. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allows the State and National Commissions to declare unfair contract terms null and void.

questions.question: In Brojo Nath Ganguly the termination rule was struck down chiefly because

options.A: it gave an unguided power to terminate on notice, without reasons, in a bargain of grossly unequal strength
options.B: it fixed a notice period shorter than the period prescribed by the Industrial Disputes Act
options.C: it had not been signed by each employee individually and was therefore void for want of consent
options.D: it was inconsistent with the doctrine of undue influence under section 16 because the corporation dominated the employees' wills

questions.explanation: The Court found the rule unconscionable and violative of section 23 and Article 14 because of the inequality of bargaining power and the absence of reasons.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B uses the undue influence doctrine, which the passage keeps separate. Option C imports a statutory notice period that is not in the passage. Option D invents a consent defect.
questions.clat_trap: Undue influence and unconscionability sound close, but the passage distinguishes them.
questions.language_trick: 'chiefly' asks for the main ground, not any possible ground.

questions.question: A private bank inserts a very harsh penal clause in a standard-form loan contract. The borrower invokes Brojo Nath and Article 14 to attack the clause. On the passage, the Article 14 route

options.A: is unavailable, and section 23 too, since unfair terms are not covered by public policy
options.B: is available because Brojo Nath extended Article 14 to every party with greater bargaining power
options.C: is unavailable against a private party, although section 23 may still be argued
options.D: is available, since all standard-form contracts are subject to Article 14

questions.explanation: The passage ties Article 14 to cases where a State instrumentality is a party. A private bank is not one, though section 23 can still be argued.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A extends Article 14 to private contracts. Option B misreads Brojo Nath's scope. Option D wrongly removes section 23 as well.
questions.clat_trap: The case concerned a government company, but its reasoning on bargaining power sounds general.
questions.language_trick: 'where a State instrumentality is a party' is the limiting phrase.

questions.question: A buyer agrees that Rs 10 lakh will be forfeited on breach. The seller suffers a provable loss of Rs 2 lakh. On Fateh Chand and Kailash Nath as described, the seller can recover

options.A: the whole Rs 10 lakh, because the parties fixed it in advance and section 74 treats it as binding
options.B: Rs 10 lakh, because proof of loss is never required under section 74
options.C: nothing, because a forfeiture clause is void under section 23
options.D: no more than the proved loss, since the named sum is only a ceiling and the loss can be proved

questions.explanation: The named sum is a ceiling. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved, so recovery is limited to reasonable compensation reflecting the proved loss.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats the stipulated sum as binding. Option B uses 'never', which Kailash Nath contradicts. Option C treats the clause as void, which the passage does not say.
questions.clat_trap: Many candidates remember 'liquidated damages are recoverable' and choose the full sum without noticing the ceiling and the proof requirement.
questions.language_trick: 'ceiling' and 'can be proved' together decide the answer.

questions.question: The Law Commission's 199th Report is best described as

options.A: a guideline binding on all courts under Article 141 of the Constitution
options.B: a binding direction that unfair terms are void under the Contract Act from the date of its publication
options.C: a recommendation for legislation, changing no law unless Parliament acts
options.D: an amendment to section 23 of the Contract Act made by the Commission itself

questions.explanation: A Law Commission report is a recommendation. The passage says the Act has no general doctrine of unfair terms.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives the report binding force. Option B treats a report as an amendment. Option D gives it the status of a judgment.
questions.clat_trap: Committee and Commission reports are persuasive only, a point that this set tests repeatedly.
questions.language_trick: 'recommended legislation' is the operative phrase.

questions.question: A buyer signs a harsh standard-form contract in a shop, with no negotiation, but the retailer holds no position of dominance over the buyer beyond ordinary superiority in bargaining. Under section 16 as described, undue influence

options.A: is made out, since the terms were unfair and the contract was in a standard form drawn up by one side
options.B: is made out, because the buyer had no real option but to sign the form presented to him by the retailer
options.C: is not made out by harsh terms alone; a dominant position and its use must be shown
options.D: is not made out, since section 16 is confined to relations of blood or marriage

questions.explanation: Section 16 as described needs a position to dominate the will and use of it to gain an unfair advantage. Harshness alone is not enough.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A and Option B treat unfairness as sufficient. Option D invents a limitation to family relations.
questions.clat_trap: Unconscionability and undue influence are merged in the wrong options, and the passage says courts distinguish them.
questions.language_trick: 'and use that position' is a second requirement that students skip.

questions.question: Assertion (A): A District Commission can declare an unfair contract term null and void under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Reason (R): The Act allows the State and National Commissions to declare unfair contract terms null and void.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: The passage names only the State and National Commissions, so A is false, while R is true.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A attributes the power to the District Commission. R is true, so the option that treats R as false does not fit.
questions.clat_trap: R is true and is a truthful statement of the passage, but A quietly swaps in a different body. A student who reads R and nods stops before checking A.
questions.language_trick: 'a District Commission' replaces 'State and National Commissions'.

passages.title: Electronic Evidence: Law Commission Reports, Section 65B and the Anvar-Arjun Panditrao Line
passages.passage: The Law Commission of India examined the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 in its 69th Report (1977) and again in its 185th Report (2003), and the Information Technology Act, 2000 inserted Sections 65A and 65B into the Act to govern electronic records. Section 65B makes a computer output admissible as a document if its conditions are met, and requires a certificate that identifies the electronic record and the device, signed by a person in a responsible position. In Anvar P V v P K Basheer (2014), a three-judge Bench held that secondary electronic evidence, such as a compact disc, cannot be proved except through a Section 65B certificate, and overruled the contrary view in State (NCT of Delhi) v Navjot Sandhu (2005). In Shafhi Mohammad v State of Himachal Pradesh (2018), a two-judge Bench held that the certificate is a procedural requirement which can be dispensed with where the party holding the device is unable to produce it. In Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020), a three-judge Bench overruled Shafhi Mohammad and held that the certificate is a condition precedent to the admissibility of secondary electronic evidence. It added that the certificate may be produced at any stage before the trial concludes, and that courts may direct its production where it is wrongly withheld. The Court also noted that where the original device is itself produced in court by the person who owns and operates it, the original is primary evidence and no certificate is needed. Section 45A permits the court to take the opinion of the Examiner of Electronic Evidence. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in force from 1 July 2024, retains the certificate requirement in a Schedule that also provides for an expert's certificate (verify the provision numbers before citing them). A Law Commission report is persuasive only; the binding law is the statute as read by the Supreme Court.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly traces the line of authority on the Section 65B certificate?

options.A: Anvar made the certificate necessary, Shafhi Mohammad relaxed it, and Arjun Panditrao restored it by overruling Shafhi Mohammad
options.B: Shafhi Mohammad overruled Anvar, and Arjun Panditrao left both decisions standing as operating at different stages of the trial
options.C: Anvar and Shafhi Mohammad both required the certificate, and Arjun Panditrao later relaxed it for owners of the device in question
options.D: Navjot Sandhu made the certificate necessary, Anvar relaxed that rule, and Arjun Panditrao affirmed the relaxation introduced in Anvar

questions.explanation: Anvar overruled Navjot Sandhu and required the certificate. Shafhi Mohammad relaxed it. Arjun Panditrao overruled Shafhi Mohammad and restored the requirement.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B reverses the roles of Navjot Sandhu and Anvar. Option C makes Shafhi Mohammad agree with Anvar, which it did not. Option D claims Shafhi overruled Anvar, but it was the other way around in effect, and Arjun Panditrao overruled Shafhi.
questions.clat_trap: Four cases are strung together and each option rearranges the same names, so a student who remembers only that 'the certificate is mandatory' cannot tell the orders apart.
questions.language_trick: 'overruling' versus 'relaxing' are the key verbs; the sequence depends on who overruled whom.

questions.question: A complainant produces in court the mobile phone which he owns and operates, and which holds a recorded conversation. The recording is being used to prove the conversation itself. On the passage, the position is that

options.A: the recording is admissible without a certificate only if the opposing party concedes that the device belongs to the complainant
options.B: the recording needs a certificate in every case, but the court may excuse the certificate where the phone has been seized by police
options.C: the recording is secondary evidence, since any electronic record is a copy, and so is inadmissible without a certificate
options.D: the original device is primary evidence, so no Section 65B certificate is required for the recording held on it

questions.explanation: The Court in Arjun Panditrao noted that where the original device is produced by its owner and operator, it is primary evidence and the certificate is unnecessary.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats all electronic records as copies, ignoring the primary evidence limb. Option B adds a concession requirement that the passage does not mention. Option C says the certificate is needed in all cases and imports an exception about police seizure that the passage does not state.
questions.clat_trap: Students who have memorised 'certificate is mandatory' apply it to every electronic item and miss that the rule concerns secondary evidence.
questions.language_trick: 'secondary evidence' in the rule versus 'original device' in the facts; the rule is not about all electronic items.

questions.question: The prosecution relies on a compact disc and files it without a Section 65B certificate. Evidence is still going on and the trial has not concluded. According to the passage,

options.A: the disc is permanently inadmissible, because the certificate must have been filed together with the disc at the very first stage of the case
options.B: the certificate can still be produced before trial ends, and the court may direct production if it is withheld
options.C: the disc is admissible without any certificate, because the court may call for the original device at any later date
options.D: the certificate can be produced only if the accused consents, since late production would prejudice a fair trial and the defence

questions.explanation: Arjun Panditrao allows the certificate to be produced at any stage before the trial concludes and lets courts direct production where it is wrongly withheld.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A imposes a filing-time bar that the Court declined to impose. Option C drops the certificate rule altogether. Option D makes the accused's consent a condition, which the Court did not require.
questions.clat_trap: 'Condition precedent' sounds like a rigid, once-only filing requirement, and students over-read it into a timing bar.
questions.language_trick: 'condition precedent to admissibility' does not mean 'condition to filing'; the timing is stated separately.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT consistent with the decision in Arjun Panditrao as described in the passage?

options.A: The certificate is a mere formality that may be waived when the device owner cannot produce it
options.B: The earlier decision in Shafhi Mohammad no longer represents the law on the point of the certificate
options.C: Courts may direct a party to produce the certificate where it is wrongly being withheld from the record
options.D: For secondary electronic evidence the certificate is a condition precedent to admissibility under Section 65B

questions.explanation: The first statement is the Shafhi Mohammad view, which Arjun Panditrao overruled. The other three are statements of the Arjun Panditrao position.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D each state something the later Bench said or implied, so they are consistent.
questions.clat_trap: A 'NOT consistent' stem asks for the false statement, and the false statement is the one that was once good law.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT consistent' reverses the usual hunt for the true option.

questions.question: Assertion (A): Because Anvar described a compact disc as an example, the certificate requirement under Section 65B applies only to compact discs and not to any other secondary electronic evidence. Reason (R): Anvar held that secondary electronic evidence such as a compact disc cannot be proved except through a Section 65B certificate.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is a correct statement of Anvar. A is false: 'such as' introduces an example, so the requirement covers secondary electronic evidence generally.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A converts an illustration into a limitation. R is accurate but does not support A.
questions.clat_trap: A true-looking reason is attached to a false assertion, tempting a 'both true' choice.
questions.language_trick: 'such as' marks an example, not a boundary.

questions.question: A student argues that now that the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 has replaced the Evidence Act, the 185th Report and the decision in Arjun Panditrao are irrelevant to the certificate. The best reply from the passage is that

options.A: the report is binding on the courts for any law that replaces the Evidence Act, so it applies to the new Act automatically as a source of rules
options.B: the decision lapsed on repeal, but the report has become binding law because the new Act has absorbed its recommendations in full
options.C: the new Act retains the certificate requirement, so the Court's reading remains strong guidance, whereas the report stays merely persuasive
options.D: both are irrelevant now because the new Act requires an expert's certificate in place of the certificate of the device operator

questions.explanation: The passage says the new Act retains the certificate requirement and that a Law Commission report is persuasive only, while the Court's reading of the statute is binding law.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A treats a report as binding, contrary to the passage. Option B wrongly assumes the report became law and the decision lapsed, although the requirement continues. Option D misreads the Schedule, which provides for an expert's certificate in addition to the existing certificate.
questions.clat_trap: Repeal looks like it wipes out case law, but the retained requirement keeps the earlier reading relevant. This is a 'persuasive versus binding' trap.
questions.language_trick: 'in addition' (a Schedule that also provides) differs from 'in place of'.

passages.subject_area: Constitutional Law (Constituent Assembly and Constitutional Review)
passages.title: From Drafting Committee to Fundamental Duties: Committees that Shaped the Constitution
passages.passage: The Constituent Assembly worked mainly through committees. The Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947, set out the aims of the Constitution. The Union Powers Committee was chaired by Nehru, and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas was chaired by Sardar Patel, with a Sub-Committee on Fundamental Rights under J B Kripalani and another on Minorities under H C Mukherjee. The Drafting Committee, set up on 29 August 1947 with B R Ambedkar as Chairman, prepared the draft that the Assembly debated clause by clause. Decades later, the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended fundamental duties, and the Forty-second Amendment inserted Part IV-A and Article 51A; the Eighty-sixth Amendment later added a duty of parents and guardians to provide opportunities for education to children between six and fourteen years. In AIIMS Students' Union v AIIMS (2001), the Court held that fundamental duties are not enforceable by writ against a citizen on their own, though they guide interpretation and remind citizens of the balance between rights and obligations. In Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v State of Uttar Pradesh (1986), Article 51A(g) was invoked alongside other grounds in a case about limestone quarrying in the Doon valley, and in Bijoe Emmanuel v State of Kerala (1986) the Court protected students who respectfully stood silent during the national anthem. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (the Venkatachaliah Commission, 2000-02) made proposals which include a fundamental right to education and a limit on the size of the Council of Ministers; the Eighty-sixth and Ninety-first Amendments followed. In Kesavananda Bharati, the Court referred to the Constituent Assembly debates in interpreting the amending power. A committee's view, in the Assembly or later, is persuasive and does not bind the Court.

questions.question: Which pairing of body and chairman or head is correct on the passage?

options.A: The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas under Jawaharlal Nehru, with the Sub-Committee on Minorities under J B Kripalani
options.B: The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas under Sardar Patel, with the Sub-Committee on Minorities under H C Mukherjee
options.C: The Union Powers Committee under Sardar Patel, with the Sub-Committee on Fundamental Rights under H C Mukherjee
options.D: The Drafting Committee under Jawaharlal Nehru, with the Sub-Committee on Fundamental Rights under J B Kripalani

questions.explanation: Patel chaired the Advisory Committee and Mukherjee headed the Minorities Sub-Committee.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A swaps both leaders. Option C swaps Patel and Nehru and also the sub-committee heads. Option D has the right sub-committee head for fundamental rights but the wrong Chairman of the Drafting Committee.
questions.clat_trap: Each wrong option is half right, so a partial memory of the names is not enough. The checking has to cover both halves of each pairing.
questions.language_trick: 'with' joins two claims; both must be right.

questions.question: Which statement about fundamental duties is correct on the passage?

options.A: They make every fundamental right conditional on performance of duties, as the Court held in the case of AIIMS Students' Union
options.B: They do not by themselves ground a writ against a citizen, though the Court uses them to guide interpretation alongside other grounds
options.C: They formed part of the Constitution as originally framed, and the Swaran Singh Committee only rearranged them into a separate Part
options.D: They are enforceable by writ against citizens, as the Doon valley quarrying case shows, because Article 51A(g) was applied there directly

questions.explanation: AIIMS Students' Union held that duties are not enforceable by writ alone but guide interpretation, and Article 51A(g) was invoked alongside other grounds in the Doon valley case.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A overreads the Doon valley case, in which the duty was invoked alongside other grounds. Option C is wrong because Part IV-A came through the Forty-second Amendment. Option D says rights are conditional on duties, whereas the Court spoke of balance and reminders.
questions.clat_trap: The Doon valley case seems to prove enforceability, but the passage says the duty was invoked 'alongside other grounds'.
questions.language_trick: 'alongside' and 'on their own' decide between a free-standing and a supporting role.

questions.question: A residents' group files a writ petition against a private quarry, relying only on the duty under Article 51A(g) to protect the natural environment and citing no statute or other fundamental right. On the passage, the likely outcome is that

options.A: the petition faces difficulty, since the duty is not enforceable alone, though it can reinforce other grounds as in the Doon valley case
options.B: the petition succeeds only if Parliament has first enacted a law bringing Part IV-A into operation against citizens
options.C: the petition fails because Article 51A(g) is addressed only to the State and cannot be applied to a private quarry in any manner
options.D: the petition succeeds, because the Doon valley case turned Article 51A(g) into a free-standing right enforceable against private persons such as the quarry owner

questions.explanation: Duties are not enforceable by writ on their own, but they guide interpretation and can support other grounds.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B wrongly makes the duty free-standing. Option C wrongly says the duty is addressed only to the State, whereas it is a duty of citizens. Option D adds a condition about a Parliamentary law that the passage does not mention.
questions.clat_trap: The petition has a sympathetic purpose and a real precedent, which tempts the student to choose success. The legal question is the standalone use of a duty.
questions.language_trick: 'only' and 'alone' in the stem control the answer.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage on the Venkatachaliah Commission?

options.A: Its recommendations bound Parliament, which had to enact them through the 86th and 91st Amendments
options.B: Its proposals included a fundamental right to education and a limit on the size of the Council of Ministers
options.C: It reviewed the working of the Constitution during the years 2000 to 2002 as a national commission
options.D: Amendments dealing with education and the size of the Council of Ministers followed its proposals

questions.explanation: The passage says that a committee's view is persuasive and does not bind, so Parliament was not bound. The other statements are made in the passage.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B, Option C and Option D are all stated or implied by the passage.
questions.clat_trap: The correct option contains a true-looking sequence of events ('followed') and quietly changes it into an obligation.
questions.language_trick: 'followed' describes sequence; 'bound to enact' states obligation.

questions.question: Consider the following statements: I. The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with B R Ambedkar as its Chairman. II. The Objectives Resolution was adopted on 13 December 1946. III. The Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation on duties was given effect by the Forty-second Amendment. IV. The Eighty-sixth Amendment added a duty of parents or guardians relating to education of children. Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, III and IV only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, II, III and IV

questions.explanation: Statement I, III and IV are stated in the passage. Statement II is wrong, since the resolution was moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: II confuses moving with adopting. Choosing all four ignores that error; choosing I and III omits the IV statement.
questions.clat_trap: A date that is nearly right (moved versus adopted) is placed among three correct statements.
questions.language_trick: 'moved' and 'adopted' are different acts with different dates.

questions.question: A litigant argues that because the Drafting Committee's draft omitted a particular right, the Court must hold that no such right exists in the Constitution. Taking the passage as a whole, the best response is that

options.A: the Court is barred from looking at the Constituent Assembly debates, as Kesavananda Bharati did not rely on them
options.B: the Court is bound by the intention of the Drafting Committee, since it prepared the draft which the Assembly debated
options.C: the Court may use Assembly material and committee views to understand the text, but they are persuasive, and the Court weighs them with the text and structure
options.D: the Court may rely on the omission only if the Drafting Committee's decision was unanimous and recorded in the debates

questions.explanation: Kesavananda Bharati referred to the debates, and the passage says that a committee's view, in the Assembly or later, is persuasive and does not bind.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A makes a committee's view binding. Option B claims the Court cannot consult the debates, contradicting the passage on Kesavananda. Option D invents a unanimity condition.
questions.clat_trap: The omission argument sounds structured and historical, tempting a student to treat the drafters' silence as decisive.
questions.language_trick: 'persuasive' and 'binds' are opposites; 'barred' and 'bound' are both too absolute.

passages.title: Administrative Reforms Commissions, the RTI Act and the Courts
passages.passage: The First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), chaired by Morarji Desai, recommended the institutions of Lokpal and Lokayukta to deal with citizens' grievances against administrative action, and the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 gave effect to that idea decades later. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2005), chaired by Veerappa Moily, began its series with a report titled 'Right to Information: Master Key to Good Governance', and the Right to Information Act, 2005 followed. The Supreme Court had earlier read the right to know into Article 19(1)(a) in S P Gupta v Union of India (1982), and in Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) applied it to voters. In CBSE v Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), the Court said that transparency must be balanced against confidentiality and that the Act cannot be used to paralyse the administration. In Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v Central Information Commissioner (2012), it held that service records of an employee are personal information exempt under Section 8(1)(j) unless a larger public interest is shown. In Central Public Information Officer, Supreme Court of India v Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019), a five-judge Bench held that the office of the Chief Justice of India is a public authority under the Act, that transparency does not undermine judicial independence, and that the privacy exemption must be applied with proportionality, weighing the public interest against harm to the individual. In Anjali Bhardwaj v Union of India (2019), the Court directed that vacancies in the Information Commissions be filled. The Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019 empowered the Centre to fix the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, which critics said weakened their independence. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has also been described as amending Section 8(1)(j) (verify). A Commission's report does not bind the Government, and the Act is the source of enforceable rights.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly links a Commission with the law that followed from its work?

options.A: Both Commissions proposed Lokpal and Lokayukta, and the Act of 2013 was passed after the Second Commission's first report on information
options.B: The First Administrative Reforms Commission recommended a statutory right to information, which led to the Act of 2005 without any later commission
options.C: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission proposed Lokpal and Lokayukta, and the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 followed in the same year as its report
options.D: The First Administrative Reforms Commission proposed Lokpal and Lokayukta, and the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 gave effect to the idea decades later

questions.explanation: The First Commission (1966) proposed the institutions and the 2013 Act followed decades later. The Second Commission began with the report on information.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A gives the Lokpal idea to the Second Commission and says the Act came in the same year. Option B gives the right to information to the First Commission. Option C makes both Commissions propose Lokpal, which the passage does not say.
questions.clat_trap: The two Commissions, two Acts and two chairmen can be shuffled in many ways, so each option is half true.
questions.language_trick: 'First' and 'Second' and 'decades later' fix the pairing.

questions.question: An applicant seeks the performance appraisal and disciplinary records of a government clerk and shows no larger public interest. On the passage, the request is

options.A: likely to be refused as personal information under Section 8(1)(j), unless a larger public interest in disclosure is shown
options.B: bound to be granted, since the privacy exemption has no application after the decision on the office of the Chief Justice of India
options.C: bound to be granted, because every document held by a public authority is a public record under the Right to Information Act
options.D: refused absolutely, since the personal information exemption allows no weighing of public interest even for a public servant

questions.explanation: Girish Ramchandra Deshpande treats service records as personal information exempt under Section 8(1)(j) unless a larger public interest is shown.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B ignores the exemptions. Option C misreads Subhash Chandra Agarwal, which required proportionality in applying the privacy exemption. Option D makes the exemption absolute, whereas the larger public interest test applies.
questions.clat_trap: The case on the CJI's office is the headline decision on transparency, and it pulls a student towards disclosure. The facts, though, concern a clerk's record.
questions.language_trick: 'unless' creates an exception to an exemption.

questions.question: In Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2019), the Court held that

options.A: the privacy exemption always outweighs public interest in matters of personal records, since proportionality was rejected as a test
options.B: the Chief Justice's office is a public authority, judicial independence is not undermined by transparency, and the privacy exemption is applied with proportionality
options.C: the Chief Justice's office is a public authority because the Act was amended in 2019 to include it expressly as a named authority
options.D: the Chief Justice's office is a public authority only for administrative matters, because judicial functions are outside the Act altogether

questions.explanation: The Bench held that the office is a public authority under the Act, that transparency does not undermine judicial independence, and that the privacy exemption involves weighing public interest against harm.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A adds a limitation to administrative matters that the passage does not mention. Option C invents a 2019 amendment; the 2019 Amendment concerned the tenure and salary of Commissioners. Option D reverses the proportionality holding with 'always'.
questions.clat_trap: The 2019 date of the decision and the 2019 Amendment are two different events, and the option merges them.
questions.language_trick: 'always' and 'only' in the wrong options signal overstatement.

questions.question: The principle in CBSE v Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011) is best stated as

options.A: the Act applies only to documents that a public authority chooses to publish voluntarily on its own initiative
options.B: the right to information is genuine but is balanced against confidentiality, and it cannot be used to paralyse administration
options.C: the right to information under Article 19(1)(a) is absolute, so the Act overrides every duty of confidentiality in public bodies
options.D: confidentiality in administration overrides the Act, which merely records a directive principle and creates no enforceable right

questions.explanation: The Court balanced transparency against confidentiality and warned against using the Act to paralyse the administration.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A makes the right absolute. Option C makes the Act unenforceable, contradicting the passage which says the Act is the source of enforceable rights. Option D limits the Act to voluntary disclosure.
questions.clat_trap: Options that go to an extreme on either side are traps in a balancing case.
questions.language_trick: 'absolute' and 'only' are red flags.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019, by allowing the Centre to fix the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, has been criticised as weakening their independence. Reason (R): In Anjali Bhardwaj v Union of India (2019), the Supreme Court directed the Centre to fix the tenure of Information Commissioners.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: A is stated in the passage. R is false, since Anjali Bhardwaj directed that vacancies in the Commissions be filled and did not direct the Centre to fix tenure.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: R gives the right case name and the right year but a wrong direction. A is accurate.
questions.clat_trap: A true assertion is paired with a reason that borrows the same year and subject, which makes it look like an explanation.
questions.language_trick: 'fix the tenure' versus 'fill vacancies'.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the sources of authority in this area is most accurate?

options.A: The right to know has constitutional roots in Article 19(1)(a), but the procedures and exemptions are set by the Act, so a challenge to the Act is tested against the Constitution and not against a Commission's report
options.B: Since the Act is a statute, the constitutional right to know recognised in S P Gupta ceased to exist when the Act was passed
options.C: Because the right to know is constitutional, the exemptions in the Act can never be applied to any citizen's request for information
options.D: A Commission's report is the source of enforceable rights, and the Act merely records what the report recommended in 2005

questions.explanation: The Court read the right to know into Article 19(1)(a), the Act supplies the procedure and exemptions, and a Commission's report does not bind the Government.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B treats the report as the source of rights. Option C uses 'never', which ignores the exemptions applied in Girish Ramchandra Deshpande. Option D says a statute wipes out the constitutional right.
questions.clat_trap: Three sources are in play (the Constitution, the Act, the Commission) and each wrong option promotes the wrong one.
questions.language_trick: 'source' versus 'recommendation' separates binding from persuasive.

passages.subject_area: Constitutional Law and Family Law (Uniform Civil Code)
passages.title: Article 44 and the Uniform Civil Code: Law Commission Views and Judicial Observations
passages.passage: Article 44, a Directive Principle, provides that the State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a uniform civil code throughout India. Matters such as marriage and divorce and wills and succession lie in the Concurrent List, so both Parliament and the State legislatures may legislate on them, subject to Article 254. In Mohd Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum (1985), the Court described Article 44 as a dead letter. In Sarla Mudgal v Union of India (1995), the Court held that a Hindu husband who converts to Islam to marry again does not dissolve his first marriage and remains liable for bigamy, and it urged the Government to consider a common code. In John Vallamattom v Union of India (2003), a provision of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 restricting Christians' bequests for religious or charitable purposes was struck down. In Jose Paulo Coutinho v Maria Luiza Valentina Pereira (2019), the Court called Goa a shining example of a State with a uniform civil code, although the Goa Civil Code is a Portuguese-era law that retains some distinctions between communities. The 21st Law Commission, in a consultation paper of August 2018, said that a uniform civil code was neither necessary nor desirable at that stage and recommended reform within each personal law. The 22nd Law Commission, in June 2023, invited fresh views from the public. Uttarakhand enacted a Uniform Civil Code Act in 2024 and brought it into force on 27 January 2025, requiring registration of marriages and of live-in relationships (verify the status of pending challenges). A Law Commission paper is advisory and does not bind the Government. Directive Principles cannot be enforced by courts, but under Article 37 they are fundamental in the governance of the country.

questions.question: What did the 21st Law Commission's consultation paper of August 2018 say about a uniform civil code?

options.A: It was neither necessary nor desirable at that stage, and reform should proceed within each personal law
options.B: Parliament must enact it immediately, because Article 44 is binding on the State and enforceable in a court of law
options.C: It was necessary but should await the report of the following Commission, and no reform of personal laws is advisable meanwhile
options.D: It should be introduced first for all communities in a single stage, leaving only Goa's civil code untouched

questions.explanation: The 2018 paper said a code was neither necessary nor desirable at that stage and recommended reform within personal laws.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B makes Article 44 binding, against Article 37. Option C invents a staged introduction. Option D calls the code necessary, which reverses the paper.
questions.clat_trap: The 2023 invitation for fresh views and the 2018 conclusion are easily mixed, and 'necessary' reverses the paper.
questions.language_trick: 'neither ... nor' is a double negative; the options flip it.

questions.question: A Hindu husband, married under the Hindu Marriage Act, converts to Islam and marries a second woman while his first wife is alive and the marriage has not been dissolved. On the passage, he is

options.A: liable only if the second wife files a complaint, since bigamy is not an offence unless the second spouse objects
options.B: liable for bigamy, since the conversion did not dissolve his first marriage
options.C: not liable until a uniform civil code is enacted, since Article 44 must first be implemented before any liability arises
options.D: not liable, as the conversion brings him under Muslim personal law and the first marriage stands dissolved in that way

questions.explanation: Sarla Mudgal held that conversion does not dissolve the first marriage and the husband remains liable for bigamy.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states the argument that was rejected in Sarla Mudgal. Option C makes liability depend on implementation of Article 44, which is not a precondition. Option D invents a complaint requirement.
questions.clat_trap: The religion-conversion angle seems to change the governing law, which is exactly the argument which the Court rejected.
questions.language_trick: 'does not dissolve' and 'remains liable' are the operative words.

questions.question: A State legislature wishes to enact a common law on marriage and succession for all its residents. On the passage, which statement is best supported?

options.A: It may not legislate at all, since only Parliament can legislate on a code that Article 44 requires 'throughout India' for the entire territory
options.B: It may legislate freely, since Concurrent List entries cannot conflict with Central laws once a State has exercised the power to legislate
options.C: It may legislate on those subjects, since they are in the Concurrent List, with repugnancy to Central law handled under Article 254
options.D: It may legislate only after a Law Commission has recommended a uniform code and the recommendation has been tabled in the legislature

questions.explanation: Marriage, divorce, wills and succession are in the Concurrent List, so State legislatures can legislate subject to Article 254.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reads 'throughout India' as an exclusive Parliamentary power. Option B adds a Law Commission condition. Option D wrongly says repugnancy cannot arise.
questions.clat_trap: 'Throughout India' in Article 44 seems to demand a national legislature, but legislative competence is decided by the Lists.
questions.language_trick: 'subject to Article 254' is the qualifier that the wrong options drop.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Uttarakhand Uniform Civil Code Act is NOT supported by the passage?

options.A: It requires registration of marriages and also of live-in relationships within the State of Uttarakhand, as the passage records
options.B: Its operation extends to every other State through Article 44 once it is in force in Uttarakhand
options.C: It was enacted by the State in the year 2024 and was brought into force in the following year, making Uttarakhand the first State to do so
options.D: It came into force on 27 January 2025 and so Uttarakhand became the first State to bring such a code into force

questions.explanation: The passage says nothing to suggest the Act applies outside Uttarakhand. Article 44 does not extend a State law to other States.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A, Option C and Option D are each stated in the passage; Option C is a fair reading of the passage's date, and it is the first State only in the sense reported.
questions.clat_trap: A false statement sits among three true ones, and its confidence is borrowed from the mention of Article 44.
questions.language_trick: 'NOT supported' reverses the search.

questions.question: Assertion (A): The observation in Jose Paulo Coutinho that Goa is a shining example of a uniform civil code shows that the Goa Civil Code is free of any distinction between communities. Reason (R): The passage notes that the Goa Civil Code retains some distinctions between communities.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is stated in the passage. A is false because the Goa Civil Code retains some distinctions, and the Court's phrase was an observation.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A overstates the observation. R is true but contradicts A, so it cannot explain it.
questions.clat_trap: The praise of Goa is taken for a finding of fact about its law.
questions.language_trick: 'free of any distinction' is absolute while the passage says 'retains some distinctions'.

questions.question: Which of the following is best treated as the decision (ratio) in the cases in the passage, as opposed to a mere observation by the Court?

options.A: In Sarla Mudgal, the Court urged the Government to consider a common code as a way of avoiding misuse of conversion
options.B: In John Vallamattom, the provision of the Indian Succession Act restricting Christians' bequests for religious or charitable purposes was struck down
options.C: In Coutinho, the Court called Goa a shining example of a State that has a uniform civil code in force
options.D: In Shah Bano, the Court described Article 44 as a dead letter while dealing with maintenance for a divorced Muslim wife

questions.explanation: Striking down a provision decides the dispute before the Court. The descriptions of Article 44 as a dead letter, the urging of the Government and the praise of Goa are observations that were not necessary for the result.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A is a description of Article 44. Option C is an appeal to the Government and not the holding on bigamy. Option D is praise that was not needed for the decision.
questions.clat_trap: Famous quotations are not always the ratio. Students pick them because they are well known.
questions.language_trick: 'urged' and 'called' are words used for observations; 'struck down' marks a decision.

passages.subject_area: Medical Law, Torts and Constitutional Law
passages.title: End-of-Life Law and Medical Negligence: Law Commission Reports and Judicial Guidelines
passages.passage: The Law Commission of India, in its 196th Report (2006) on medical treatment of terminally ill patients and its 241st Report (2012), recommended legal protection for withholding or withdrawing treatment and protection for doctors who act in good faith. In Gian Kaur v State of Punjab (1996), a five-judge Bench held that there is no right to die under Article 21 and upheld Section 309 of the Indian Penal Code and the offence of abetment of suicide, but observed that a right to die with dignity in the case of a terminally ill patient in an irreversible condition may be part of the right to life. In Aruna Shanbaug v Union of India (2011), the Court permitted passive euthanasia for a patient in a persistent vegetative state, with the approval of the High Court. In Common Cause v Union of India (2018), a five-judge Bench held that passive euthanasia and advance directives, or living wills, are valid under Article 21 and laid down guidelines; these were simplified in January 2023 by permitting attestation before a notary or a gazetted officer and by reconstituting the medical boards. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 presumes severe stress in a person who attempts suicide and bars punishment, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita did not retain a stand-alone offence for attempted suicide (verify). On medical negligence, in Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005), the Court held that a doctor is criminally liable only for gross negligence or recklessness, not for mere lack of care or an error of judgment, and applied the Bolam test; in Indian Medical Association v V P Shantha (1995), medical services were held to be 'service' under the Consumer Protection Act; and in Samira Kohli v Dr Prabha Manchanda (2008), the Court required informed consent for treatment beyond what was consented to. The Law Commission's recommendations are not binding; the Common Cause guidelines operate until Parliament legislates.

questions.question: What did the Court hold in Gian Kaur v State of Punjab (1996)?

options.A: Section 309 is valid and passive euthanasia is permitted in every case once the treating doctor considers it to be in the patient's interest
options.B: There is no right to die and Section 309 is valid, though dying with dignity in terminal illness may form part of Article 21
options.C: There is no right to die and no scope at all for dignity in dying, even for a terminally ill patient in an irreversible condition who can no longer recover
options.D: The right to die forms part of Article 21, so Section 309 is void, while the offence of abetment of suicide continues to stand as a separate penal provision

questions.explanation: Gian Kaur upheld Section 309 and rejected a right to die, while observing that dying with dignity of a terminally ill patient may form part of the right to life.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A states a view of the right to die that Gian Kaur rejected. Option C denies the observation on dignity, which the passage records. Option D gives a doctor's discretion that no decision in the passage supports.
questions.clat_trap: The 'right to die with dignity' phrase and the 'no right to die' holding sound contradictory, and the options exploit that.
questions.language_trick: 'no right to die' and 'right to die with dignity' are different propositions.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly states the sequence of the end-of-life decisions in the passage?

options.A: Gian Kaur recognised passive euthanasia, Aruna Shanbaug struck down Section 309, and Common Cause required Parliament to legislate first
options.B: Common Cause allowed passive euthanasia first, Aruna Shanbaug restricted it to living wills, and Gian Kaur set the guidelines in 2023
options.C: Aruna Shanbaug upheld living wills, Common Cause required High Court approval in every case, and Gian Kaur recognised a general right to die
options.D: Gian Kaur left room for dignity in dying, Aruna Shanbaug allowed passive euthanasia, and Common Cause upheld living wills

questions.explanation: The order is Gian Kaur (1996), Aruna Shanbaug (2011) and Common Cause (2018, simplified in 2023).
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A reverses the content of each decision. Option B reverses the chronology and misattributes the 2023 changes, which simplified Common Cause. Option C attributes the striking down of Section 309 to a case which did not do so.
questions.clat_trap: Three decisions, three outcomes and one 2023 modification are combined, so one error can hide in a long option.
questions.language_trick: The 2023 simplification modified Common Cause; it was not a separate case.

questions.question: A terminally ill patient executed a living will, attested by a gazetted officer after the January 2023 simplification, directing that no ventilator be used. On the passage, the directive is

options.A: valid only if it was signed before a Magistrate, because notary or gazetted officer attestation was not accepted by the Court
options.B: valid under Article 21 on the Common Cause guidelines as simplified, with the medical boards deciding on its implementation
options.C: invalid, since only Parliament can recognise advance directives and the Common Cause guidelines lapsed in January 2023
options.D: invalid unless the High Court approves it, as in Aruna Shanbaug, since Common Cause concerned only patients in a vegetative state

questions.explanation: Common Cause upheld living wills and the 2023 modification permitted attestation by a notary or a gazetted officer and reconstituted the medical boards.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A extends the Aruna Shanbaug requirement of High Court approval to living wills. Option C says the guidelines lapsed, whereas they operate until Parliament legislates. Option D contradicts the passage on attestation.
questions.clat_trap: Aruna Shanbaug is the better-known case and tempts a student to apply High Court approval where a living will is in issue.
questions.language_trick: 'simplified' in 2023 signals a lighter procedure, not a lapse.

questions.question: A surgeon chooses a course of treatment accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion. The patient dies, and the surgeon is later shown to have made an honest error of judgment. On the passage, the surgeon is

options.A: criminally liable, because the Bolam test governs only civil claims for damages and does not apply to criminal cases
options.B: criminally liable, since any negligence that results in the death of a patient is criminal negligence by a medical practitioner
options.C: not criminally liable, since only gross negligence or recklessness attracts criminal liability and an error of judgment does not
options.D: not criminally liable only if the patient had given written consent to the course of treatment that was chosen

questions.explanation: Jacob Mathew requires gross negligence or recklessness for criminal liability and applied the Bolam test.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option A drops the gross negligence standard. Option B says Bolam is irrelevant to criminal liability, though Jacob Mathew applied it. Option D adds a written consent requirement for the defence.
questions.clat_trap: Death of a patient creates a pull towards liability, but the standard for crime is higher than for civil liability.
questions.language_trick: 'only' in the correct option states the threshold.

questions.question: Assertion (A): In Samira Kohli v Dr Prabha Manchanda (2008), the Court allowed a surgeon to extend a procedure beyond the consent given, whenever the surgeon considers the extension medically beneficial. Reason (R): The Court in Samira Kohli required informed consent for treatment beyond what was consented to.

options.A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true but R is false
options.D: A is false but R is true

questions.explanation: R is stated in the passage. A contradicts R and the holding, since consent is needed for treatment beyond what was consented to.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: A turns a requirement of consent into a permission based on the doctor's view. R is correct but inconsistent with A.
questions.clat_trap: A paternalistic idea sounds medically sensible and is attached to a real case name.
questions.language_trick: 'whenever the surgeon considers' makes the doctor the judge.

questions.question: Which statement about the legal force of the sources in the passage is most accurate?

options.A: The Common Cause guidelines bind as judicial directions until Parliament legislates; Law Commission reports only persuade
options.B: The 241st Report's recommendations became law when Common Cause cited them, since a Bench's reliance converts a report into a statute
options.C: The Common Cause guidelines are merely advisory, because Parliament has not yet legislated on advance directives
options.D: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 legalised passive euthanasia and so superseded the guidelines laid down in Common Cause

questions.explanation: The passage says the Law Commission's recommendations are not binding and the Common Cause guidelines operate until Parliament legislates.
questions.why_other_options_are_wrong: Option B turns a report into a statute by citation. Option C misreads the 2017 Act, which deals with suicide attempts, as legalising passive euthanasia. Option D treats judicial guidelines as advisory.
questions.clat_trap: Reports, statutes and judicial guidelines are all 'law' in loose speech, and the stem asks which has binding force.
questions.language_trick: 'bind' versus 'persuasive' and 'merely advisory'.
